The Peaches of New York, by Hedrick with the help of Howe, Taylor, and Tubergen, is the report of the New York Agricultural Experiment Station for 1916. Albany printed the book in 1917. A letter of transmittal from Geneva, dated January 31, 1917, sends the manuscript to the station's board.

The letter calls the volume the fifth in the station's series of fruit publications. Peach growing, it says, is an important industry in the state. The peach at its best is a luscious food, adding to health as well as enjoyment. Since varieties differ greatly in quality and fitness for place, a full study of those grown in New York seemed worth while. Hedrick's fruit monographs set the standard for American pomology.
49026-schubert-and-his-work:
Herbert Peyser wrote this life of Schubert for the Philharmonic-Symphony Society of New York in 1946. Grosset and Dunlap sold the book to the wide public. Schubert and Vogl at the piano, from Schwind's drawing, heads the plates.

The most lovable and the shortest-lived of the great composers: Peyser's first line holds his whole case. Franz Schubert was doubly a paradox, he writes. Alone of the great Viennese masters he was born in Vienna itself. Yet not a drop of Viennese blood ran in him; his roots lay in Moravian and Silesian soil. His grandfather Karl was a peasant and local judge in a Neudorf there. Peyser tells the short, song-crowded life with a critic's love.
49260-the-history-of-orange-county-new-y:
Russel Headley edited The History of Orange County, New York, published at Middletown in 1909. The book divides its labour among many hands. Ten opening chapters treat the county as a whole. Town chapters follow, each written by a local author: Blooming Grove, Chester, Cornwall, Crawford, and the rest, through Warwick, Wawayanda, and Woodbury. A city history of Newburgh stands among them.

Professional chapters close the volume, on the bench and bar and on the medical profession. County histories of this kind were the standard monuments of American local pride. Farmers, lawyers, and merchants subscribed for them, and their pages preserved town records, family sketches, and memories that existed nowhere else. Headley's volume covers a Hudson Valley county of orchards, iron, and river towns. It remains a first source for genealogists and local historians working on the region north of New York City.
49440-york:
York is a topographical book described by George Benson and pictured by E W Haslehust, in the Beautiful England series. Each book of the series holds twelve reproductions of watercolour paintings by Haslehust. The frontispiece shows the water-gates at Lendal Bridge. The illustrations list Micklegate Bar, Bootham Bar, and Fishergate Postern from the walls.

The Shambles, York Minster, and the ruins of Saint Mary's Abbey are also pictured, with a plan of the cathedral. The text opens on the city itself. It would seem, Benson writes, that if there is one thing which can be done at York better almost than anywhere else in the kingdom, that thing is the realisation of history. It is in this, above all, that the charm lies. The series covered Canterbury, Oxford, the English Lakes, and many more places.
49594-the-dark:
The Dark is a tale by Leonid Andreev, in English dress by two hands, out in nineteen twenty-two. It came out at the press of a famed wife and her spouse. The tale opens on a man whose life has been a game of dire stakes. Luck has held for him in all his work, but past three days it has turned.

A fluke has given the law a clue, and shades have tracked him past two days and nights with no sleep. One by one his hid spots are cut off. On the next day but one he must throw the last bomb of a great plot, the mark of pride in his band. Worn out, he takes a hid spot of a base kind, though he has kept pure past all his years. That clash drives the tale.
49643-the-children-s-tabernacle-or-hand-:
The author known as ALOE wrote The Children's Tabernacle, or Hand-Work and Heart-Work, printed at New York in 1875. The uniform ALOE books sold at seventy-five cents each, with titles such as The Giant-Killer and The Young Pilgrim. Carter and Brothers issued the long list from Broadway.

In the preface the author asks if deep Old Testament types can be made clear and gripping to the young. Reading those types in Gospel light, she argues, matters greatly and cannot be overrated in perilous times. Parents and teachers are asked to help children join hand work with heart work in the lessons. Young readers get Bible teaching through story and craft.
49912-the-employments-of-women-a-cyclop-:
Virginia Penny published The Employments of Women in eighteen sixty-three, a guide to woman's work in the United States. She gave the book to worthy and hard-working women who were striving to earn a living. Penny notes that books on the sphere of woman were easy to find.

Good advice alone, she argues, does not feed or house anyone. Women need real pursuits opened to them, with facts on pay, training, and entry. Her guide surveys trade after trade that women held or might hold. It treats work as a plain need of the day, not as a topic for fine words.
50000-john-gutenberg-first-master-printe:
Trubner printed this life of John Gutenberg in London in 1860. Just one hundred copies were printed, Englished from the German. Chapter one tells how John Fust wed his daughter Christine away. She married Peter Schoeffer, Fust partner in the Mainz print shop.

Chapter two gives Gutenberg own words and acts at that wedding time. A little Parisian guest sparks talk in his dwelling in chapter three. Quarrels of two archbishops bring suffering on Mainz poor folk next. The book ends with Gutenberg death and his unknown, unmarked tomb at Mainz.
50048-the-diary-of-a-turk:
The Diary of a Turk, by Halil Halid, was published in London in 1903, with eight pictures. Halid gives the book to the memory of Gibb, a scholar of the East and author of a history of Ottoman poetry. Chapter one treats his home in Asia Minor.

Later chapters cover school and the harem, and women in the East. He goes to Constantinople and pursues his studies. A new profession, and the question of being drafted, follow. Heads then name Turkey internal dangers, a new costume and career, the Sultan policy, and the struggle with Young Turkey. England and the Caliphate, a spy in a bath, and flight to England close the list. Readers get a Turk own diary of home, rule, and exile.
5009-the-unspeakable-perk:
Samuel Hopkins Adams's Unspeakable Perk opens with a young man who has taken on a large contract. He hates a wide stretch of Caribbean Sea. It lies very blue, still, and indifferent to human feeling. Each day he sits in the shade of an overhanging boulder. Cool air and cool water trickle down the slope. He despises the placid ocean and wishes it would dry up so he could walk home.

In plain American terms, the young man is homesick, stranded, and furious at his exile. Adams turns that comic hatred into a romance and adventure of the tropics. Readers get a witty tale of a man at odds with paradise, learning that the sea he hates may be the least of his troubles.
51048-the-geologic-story-of-canyonlands-:
Lohman wrote this Geological Survey bulletin, number 1327, issued by the Government Printing Office in 1974. Stacy drew the graphics for the Department of the Interior volume. A photo looks north from the east wall of Devils Lane, toward Junction Butte and Grand View Point across the Colorado River.

The contents open with a new park being born in the park's story. Major Powell's river expeditions follow as the second section in the list. Cedar Mesa sandstone forms the needles in the photo caption, and Lohman explains how rivers, wind and deep time carved the canyons, mesas and needles of Utah's Canyonlands.
5142-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon's romance begins with Grenfall Lorry, a bored American traveller boarding an eastbound train at Denver. On the journey he meets strangers who draw him toward the small European principality of Graustark, where a princess, a throne, and a plot against the crown await him.

Lorry's adventure moves from railway coaches to castles, abductions, midnight flights, and a tower imprisonment, as love and loyalty pull him into Graustark's politics. The book founded a whole genre of imaginary-kingdom romance, and it remains a brisk, escapist tale for readers who enjoy Ruritanian adventure.
51909-the-apaches-of-new-york:
Alfred Henry Lewis gathered true tales of New York gangs, issued in Chicago and New York in 1912. Lewis says the tales came straight from the police, with added facts from the gang men themselves. Names, times, and places are given as real, and most events were less than three years old.

His preface warns that few tales end at Sing Sing or in the death chair. Police often know more than they can prove in court, and ward bosses shield useful voters. The first tale opens at Chick Tricker's house of call at One Hundred and Twenty-eight Park Row, where drink, music, and dance fill the night.
51912-the-boss-and-how-he-came-to-rule-n:
The Boss, and How He Came to Rule New York, by Alfred Henry Lewis, came out in New York in 1903. The book is cast as the memoirs of a retired Tammany boss who holds millions and lives in peace. He says at the start that he has no skill with a pen, so a man of print writes the pages for him.

He vows to paint no man's portrait but his own, and to shield old friends under false names. Still, he means to tell the inner history of Tammany and his own rise within it. He asks why he speaks at all, and weighs pride, remorse, and a hunger for sympathy. The result reads as a frank tour of machine rule in the city.
52390-mammals-of-mount-rainier-national-:
Mammals of Mount Rainier National Park is a park natural history handbook by Merlin K Potts and Russell K Grater. The Mount Rainier Natural History Association published it at Longmire, Washington, in 1949. Potts was assistant park naturalist and Grater park naturalist. Photographs came from several national parks and from Joseph Dixon and others.

A foreword and chapters on wildlife trends and problems open the book. The life zones of the mountain are explained before the species accounts begin. The mammals section runs from page thirteen to a hypothetical list of unconfirmed species. A bibliography closes the volume. Such handbooks taught visitors to see a park as a living system, not a backdrop. Rainier's marmots, goats, deer, and bears here receive their official natural history, zone by zone.
52634-women-s-work:
Bulley and Whitley surveyed the work open to women in a volume of the Social Questions of To-Day series. Methuen of London published it in 1894, with a preface by Lady Dilke. The first chapter treats work of the mind and of art. It sorts writing, the press, and teaching, with hours, pay, and the odds for and against each path.

Later chapters move through office and shop work, trade unions, and the cloth trades. One chapter asks what hard trades do to a woman's health, and one treats the deaths of infants. The contents name law, the care of the sick, drugs, teeth, and the stage among the fields weighed. Pay tables for school posts are given in full. The book is a sober, fact filled guide for women who had to earn a living in the 1890s.
52971-the-indians-of-carlsbad-caverns-na:
Jack R Williams wrote The Indians of Carlsbad Caverns National Park, a short book held by rights from 1956. Williams wrote from Carlsbad, in New Mexico. Phyllis Freeland Broyles drew the wrap for the book. A map shows where the groups of the land once lay.

Williams warns that the tale is hard to tell in a neat way. Its ground is not the neat lines of the park, but the Guadalupe range. More than one group lived there, and each took in ways from those round it. Parts deal with the first men, with the basket makers of the caves, and with the Mescalero Apaches. A part on the Comanches and a list of sources close the book. First folk, he says, came as small bands who chased game and gleaned seeds.
53539-road-guide-to-lassen-volcanic-nati:
Paul Schulz wrote this road guide to Lassen Volcanic National Park. The Loomis Museum Association issued it first in 1950, revised 1966. A cover photo shows Lassen Peak over Manzanita Lake in color. Numbered stakes along the road key the guide stops in order.

Stop one is the Raker Memorial at the park boundary line. Congressman Raker carried the bill that made the park in 1916. President Wilson signed it August 9 of that year, it notes. Park off the pavement, the guide warns, an accident spoils trips. Brokeoff Mountain trail starts at the second numbered stop of the road guide.
53854-forge-work:
Forge Work is a manual training textbook by William Ilgen, forging instructor at Crane Technical High School in Chicago. The American Book Company copyrighted it in 1912, with editorial revision by Charles Moore of Central High School, Newark. A photograph of a manual training forge shop fronts the lessons.

Chapter one catalogs the tools: the forge, fire tools, fuels, the anvil, hammers of every peen, sledges, and a long family of tongs. Chapter two teaches the blows and operations: drawing, bending, upsetting, twisting, and welding in its lap, cleft, butt, jump, and V forms. Practice exercises make staples, hooks, bolts, and chains, and later chapters treat tool steel, hardening, and tempering.
54212-a-modern-mephistopheles-and-a-whis:
Louisa M Alcott wrote A Modern Mephistopheles and A Whisper in the Dark, issued in Boston by Roberts Brothers in eighteen eighty nine. A Faust line heads the tale, The indescribable, here it is done, the woman soul leadeth us upward and on. Chapter one opens in a garret. Without, a midwinter twilight, where wandering snowflakes eddied in the bitter wind, it begins.

Within, a garret gloomy and bare held a dying young poet, the tale continues. A stranger offers him fame and ease at a price, in Alcott hidden sensation tale. The volume first appeared without her name, as one of her blood and thunder stories. A Whisper in the Dark, a shorter sensation tale, fills the back. Alcott wrote Moods and Work in the same list. Readers get the secret, darker Alcott behind Little Women.
54389-nelson-the-newsboy-or-afloat-in-ne:
Horatio Alger began Nelson the Newsboy, or Afloat in New York, and Arthur Winfield completed it; the book was printed in New York in 1905. Winfield had written the Rover Boys tales. A front picture shows the hero catching sight of the bully newsboy who had robbed him. A preface tells the plan: the tale relates the adventures of a wide-awake lad in the great metropolis.

The youth is of unknown parentage and is thrown on his own resources at a tender age. He becomes a newsboy first, and from that works up gradually to something better. Poverty tempts him hard to do wrong, but something in his make-up keeps him in the right path. Alger first meant the story as a drama for young people. After his death the manuscript passed to Winfield, who made it over into this volume.
54602-ancient-and-modern-furniture-and-w:
John Hungerford Pollen wrote Ancient and Modern Furniture and Woodwork, issued as number three of the South Kensington Museum Art Handbooks, edited by William Maskell. A note by the editor, dated August 1875, explains the series. The handbooks reprint the essays set before the museum's large catalogues, shortened into a handy shape. They are meant to serve other collections too, at trifling cost.

Contents open with furniture ancient and modern in one view. Egypt, Nineveh, and Greece follow, then the Romans and Byzantine art. The middle ages, the fifteenth century, and the Renaissance in Italy come next. The Renaissance in England, Flanders, France, Germany, and Spain follows, then Tudor and Stuart styles. Furniture of the eighteenth century and changes of taste close the book. An appendix names the designers of woodwork and makers of furniture.
54929-christopher-columbus-his-life-and-:
Christopher Columbus: His Life and His Work is a biography by Charles Kendall Adams, president of Cornell University, published by Dodd, Mead in 1892 in the Makers of America series. The Lotto portrait of Columbus fronts the volume. Adams's preface states his aim: to present in popular form the results of the latest researches on the life and work of Columbus.

He made constant use of the original authorities. His effort was to interpret their conflicting statements in the spirit of modern criticism. The chief sources are Columbus's own letters and journal, the history purporting to be by his son Fernando, and the historians Las Casas, Bernaldez, Oviedo, Peter Martyr, and Herrera. A passage preserved in the copy weighs the son's history. Adams could not adopt without reservation the views on the work attributed to Fernando. Harrisse's reasoning, he grants, is unquestionable in force.
55150-many-storied-mountains-the-life-of:
Many-Storied Mountains: The Life of Glacier National Park was written and photographed by Greg Beaumont. The National Park Service published it in 1978 in its Natural History Series, for sale by the Superintendent of Documents in Washington.

The book is a natural history of the park, and not a guidebook. It gives an ecological overview of the region. It is also a personal statement, a response to a rugged, delicate land. A Stoney Indian Pass photograph calls the landform a monument to moving ice. A million years ago, its caption says, Pleistocene glaciers sculptured the land. Only the higher peaks rose above the ice flowing toward the Great Plains. Beaumont thanks the chief naturalist and staff of the park, and the critic Douglas Chadwick.
55217-making-his-mark:
Making His Mark is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger, junior, of America. Penn Publishing of Philadelphia issued it in the year 1903 here. Mason drew the illustrations, and rights date to 1901 in front. A front plate shows a man who took a boy in his arms. Chapter one, An Unpleasant Talk, opens the rise of Gerald Lane.

Tubbs the grocer and Mrs Lane's disappointment fill the early heads. A lost letter, Abel's arrival in Portville, and the son and heir follow. A plebeian relative gets a cold reception in that proud house. A lucky rescue and a sympathizing friend turn Gerald's luck at last. A grocer's clerk, an artful trick, and a crisis crown the list.
55476-ships-at-work:
Mary Elting wrote Ships at Work, with drawings by Manning De V Lee, issued by Garden City Books at Garden City, New York. The copyright is nineteen forty six, with a later print in nineteen fifty three. Elting writes for young readers in clear, warm prose. Big pictures show ships, docks, and crews at their tasks. A first part is called Ships and Men.

Elting says a ship is a marvellous thing that tied the world into one round ball. Brave seamen from a thousand ports faced storms to make the world larger, then to bring folk close. A ship is always she to a seagoing man, and never a boat. Jim, a sailor on a freighter across the Atlantic, shows the work of standing watch. He is woken at half past three each morning in the forecastle. Young readers learn ship words and ship pride at once.
55482-machines-at-work:
Machines at Work is a child fact book by Mary Elting with cuts by Laszlo Roth. A Garden City house brought it out in print of nineteen fifty three. Man made giants heads its first part on the great dig scoop. That scoop tears out earth chunks more than twice a man tall in one bite. Its long arm lifts loads as high as a seven floor house.

Few such scoops stand in the world, the book tells young eyes. Coal beds near the skin of the earth are their work place by plan. Forty five freight cars bore one scoop in parts to its mine. In one span it digs as much as a vast host of men by hand. Ship yard cranes and pile hams fill more parts of the book.
55525-trains-at-work:
Mary Elting wrote this picture book about trains at work, with pictures by David Lyle Millard, copyrighted in 1953. Its first section is about Sam, the fireman on a big freight locomotive. Sam comes from a family of railroaders: his father and grandfather were locomotive engineers, and his grandmother worked a telegraph key in a station.

Railroad slang fills the pages. A locomotive was a hog, and the man who ran it the hogger, and the roundhouse where engines were cleaned was the pig-pen or the barn. Lumps of coal were black diamonds, and the fireman who shovelled them answered to diamond pusher, ashcat, bakehead, and tallow pot, and called his shovel his banjo.
56270-the-story-of-noah-s-ark:
The Story of Noah's Ark is a picture book told and illustrated by Boyd Smith, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1905. Twenty-six coloured plates carry the biblical story in short captions of mock-scriptural prose. The six-hundred-year-old Noah is warned of the flood, tells his neighbours, and is scoffed at for his trouble.

The humour is in the modern troubles that beset the ancient shipwright. Strikes delay the building: his workmen clamour for more pay and stone those who will work, and Noah must bargain and start afresh. The animals, summoned two by two, grumble that it may be but a shower and refuse to be hurried. Later plates promise the dinosaurs' dilemma, homesickness and strained relations inside the ark, the raven and the dove, and the rainbow. The deadpan mismatch of Genesis and the labour news of 1905 is the book's whole charm.
56428-saratoga-national-historical-park-:
Saratoga National Historical Park is Handbook Number Four of its line. Charles W Snell and Francis F Wilshin wrote it. The National Park Service issued it at Washington in 1950. A revised form came in 1959. The Government Printing Office printed both rounds. Copies sold for twenty-five cents each.

The British Plan of 1777 opens the contents. The Burgoyne Campaign follows at page four. Retreat of the Americans comes next in line. The Saint Leger expedition gets its own part. The Battle of Bennington fills page ten. The American line and army's make-up follow. A powder horn marks the title page art. Park handbooks like this put a whole campaign in a coat pocket, so walkers could read the ground where an army surrendered.
56831-the-king-of-the-park:
The King of the Park, by Marshall Saunders, author of Beautiful Joe, was issued by Thomas Y Crowell and Company at New York in 1897 and reached its fourth thousand. Saunders inscribes the book to Police-Sergeant Charles Wesley Hebard of the Back Bay Fens and his humane associates.

The story opens at the Boylston Street entrance to the Fens, where Sergeant Hardy watches a young lady take a bicycle lesson. Chapters introduce King Boozy, the rest of the cats, a child in trouble, and Eugene, who is arrested before a king comes to the rescue.
57576-a-method-of-tanning-without-bark:
A Method of Tanning Without Bark is a small trade tract by William Maple, printed at Dublin in 1729. It is inscribed to William Conolly, Speaker of the House of Commons of Ireland, and to the rest of the members of that house. The point of the method is in the title: to tan leather without oak bark.

The tract opens with rules of political arithmetic. The riches of a country, Maple says, arise from the produce of the earth and the labour spent in improving it. Native goods grow in step with the number of people fully and usefully at work. Every industrious person adds to the wealth of the nation, and every idler takes from it. On those grounds he builds his case for a home method that would keep Ireland's money in Ireland.
58899-journey-work:
Dave Dryfoos speaks for old men in Journey Work, from Worlds of If Science Fiction in January 1955. The blurb urges its hero on: get mad, old man, but do not give up. Somewhere there is a job youth cannot do, a dangerous job that will bring fame, fortune, and peace. The hero is Ollie Hollveg, a tomato picker past seventy.

At seventy a poor man is expected to retire to a Home for Seniles, and Ollie has dodged the geriatricians for sixteen years. In a central California field the rancher Rost short-pays the old pickers, then fires a gas gun under Ollie's nose.
59318-rodent-control-aided-by-emergency-:
Rodent Control Aided by Emergency Conservation Work is a wild life sheet of December nineteen thirty six. Stanley Young, chief of game rule for the farm board, wrote the sheet. Camp crews of the job corps gave great aid in rodent wars, it opens. West folk have fought these beasts since first claims on the plains. Crop growth needs that war as much as east fruit needs spray.

Kinds named for war span prairie dogs, ground squirrels, and pocket gophers. Kangaroo rats, rabbits, and quill pigs stand in the same war list. Old proof shows poison shipped round Cape Horn in eighteen oh eight. Land men paid for wars on their own plots while state funds lagged. Parts weigh crew drill, time fit, and shield of harm free kinds.
59482-pere-marquette-state-park:
Pere Marquette State Park, a guide to the Illinois state park and conservation area, describes a tract of bluffs above the Illinois River. The park covers over five thousand acres in Jersey County, five miles west of Grafton on Route 100. It is named for Father Jacques Marquette, the French Jesuit who, with Louis Jolliet, first entered this country in 1673. A large white cross by the road marks their landing place.

The state took the land in 1932, park and conservation area side by side. The hub is Pere Marquette Lodge, built of native stone and rustic timbers, with seven stone guest houses behind it. Its lounge holds a stone fireplace of seven hundred tons. A swimming pool, a small golf course, shuffleboard, and horseshoe courts serve the guests. Across the river lies a federal wild life refuge of more than eight thousand acres.
59836-the-geologic-story-of-glacier-nati:
The Geologic Story of Glacier National Park, by James Dyson, is Special Bulletin number three of the Glacier Natural History Association. It sold for twenty five cents. Chief Mountain shows on the cover. Dyson headed the geology and geography department at Lafayette College. He opens by shaking off the old image of the geologist as a queer fellow with a hammer. Geology, he says, is the science of the Earth.

It tells the history of the planet and of life on it. Inner forces raise, bend, and break the crust. Outer agents, water, wind, and ice, wear it down and carry it to the sea. Soil, rock, hills, lakes, and even tin cans trace back to such work. The bulletin aims that science at park visitors in plain words.
59839-vanderbilt-mansion-national-histor:
Charles W Snell wrote a handbook on the Vanderbilt Mansion National Historic Site in New York. The National Park Service issued it as historical handbook number thirty two in 1960. A reprint followed in 1961. The series describes historic and archeological areas in the National Park System. The booklet sold for sixty cents from the Superintendent of Documents.

Stewart L Udall was Secretary of the Interior and Conrad L Wirth directed the Park Service when it appeared. Such handbooks gave visitors the history and meaning of a site in brief compass. The Vanderbilt mansion at Hyde Park stood for the great Hudson River estates. Snell's text joined description of the house and grounds to the family's story.
59913-ferns-of-hawaii-national-park:
Ferns of Hawaii National Park, by Douglass Hubbard, park naturalist, came out in June 1952. It was volume 5, number 1 of Hawaii Nature Notes, the notes of the park's Naturalist Division and the Hawaii Natural History Association. The booklet is dedicated to Eugene Horner, whose love of Hawaiian ferns ran past fifty years. It sold as a special issue for fifty cents.

Hubbard is plain about his limits: some seventy fern species grow in the park, and he treats only the common ones a visitor can find near the path. Pictures stand in for stiff description, and the kinds are set in order of plenty, not of science. A short list of books points the keen reader onward. The opening pages praise the park's fern jungles and native woods, and ask visitors to help keep them unspoiled.
59978-clermont-state-historic-park-germa:
Clermont State Historic Park at Germantown, New York, is told of in a park guide that traces the Livingston estate on the Hudson River. Robert Livingston, born in Scotland and raised in the Netherlands, reached Albany in the winter of sixteen seventy four to sixteen seventy five. He grew rich in shipping and fur trade. In sixteen eighty six he gained a charter for the Manor of Livingston, with one hundred sixty two thousand acres.

His third son took thirteen thousand acres as Clermont, or the Lower Manor, in seventeen twenty eight. A mansion rose on a low flat above the Hudson near seventeen thirty. Later Robert R Livingston, the Chancellor, helped draft the Declaration of Independence work in Congress. British troops burned Clermont in seventeen seventy seven, and the house was rebuilt. The guide ties house, land, and a famed family into one Hudson tale.
60132-wild-animals-of-yellowstone-nation:
Wild Animals of Yellowstone National Park, by Harold J Brodrick, is booklet number one of the Yellowstone Interpretive Series. The Yellowstone Library and Museum Association printed it at the park in 1954, and reprinted it in March 1959. Drawings show many of the species described.

The association is a non profit body whose purpose is to stir interest in the teaching and spirit lifting sides of Yellowstone history and natural history. It is sponsored and operated by the Naturalist Division in the park. The booklet gives general information on many of the mammals most commonly seen in Yellowstone. Visitors for many years have found the larger mammals of the region of unusual interest. The demand for printed information in general terms at a reasonable cost prompted the book. Park fans get a ranger guide to bears, elk, and bison country.
60176-dancers-in-the-dark:
Dorothy Speare wrote Dancers in the Dark, published by George H Doran at New York in 1922. She dedicated the book to the girls of today. Joy Nelson comes in at half-past four in the morning, worn out from dancing all night. Her new silver slippers are killing her. The room she shares with two other girls holds no sleep. Her roommates sit on the bed, smoking, and offer her a cigarette.

Jerry, fascinating rather than pretty, has bobbed dark hair, green eyes, and a freckled face. She once chewed gum openly before a chaperone and then charged the boys a penny a chew. Sarah, all color and marcelled hair, is another sort again. Speare writes the jazz-age college girl at close range. The novel was a frank portrait of its moment.
60574-the-geologic-story-of-yellowstone-:
The Geologic Story of Yellowstone National Park is a government booklet on the geology of the Yellowstone country. It was sold by the Superintendent of Documents in Washington for a dollar and a quarter. Its subtitle calls it a review of the geologic processes and events behind the natural wonders of the region. It marks the hundredth anniversary of the oldest and largest of the national parks.

The front matter quotes Joseph Meek's account of 1829: a whole country smoking with vapour from boiling springs, with small craters whistling and blue flames and molten brimstone issuing out. The act of 1872 is printed too, setting the tract apart as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people. A photograph shows the Midway Geyser Basin. The booklet explains how fire and water made the geysers, terraces, and canyon of Yellowstone. It is science written for the park visitor.
60682-the-good-work:
Theodore Thomas wrote The Good Work, a science fiction tale from Worlds of If in February 1959. In the cities, 350 billions swarmed like termites in a hill, but Jeremiah Winthrop still called himself a man, the blurb says. Tall and rawboned, narrow of shoulder and shallow of chest, Winthrop carries dignity in every movement.

His traditions spring from rocky New England soil that nourished his forebears, buried now beneath monstrous buildings' foundations. He rides the spiral escalator up to his two-part cubicle on the one hundred and forty-eighth floor, swaying among tight, tense riders. The crowded escalator passes his floor as he steps off into the river's edge. Overpopulation fiction readers get Thomas.
60727-the-book-of-the-bayeux-tapestry-pr:
Colour copies of the full Bayeux cloth fill a Chatto and Windus volume from London in 1914. Hilaire Belloc writes the opening essay and the tale that runs with the pictures. He treats the stitched cloth as a record in pictures, one that can outlast words as speech and letters change over time.

Belloc argues that a picture speaks to the eye at once and needs no shared tongue. A few figures stand for a host, a sign marks a man, and each scene is cut to its bare core. He also weighs when the work was made and warns against loose, showy claims by past writers. Readers can then follow the Norman story scene by scene in colour.
60730-the-geology-of-darling-state-park:
Harry W Dodge Junior wrote The Geology of Darling State Park. The Vermont Geological Survey issued it in 1967. Charles G Doll served as state geologist then. Burke Mountain stands as the park's great peak. A cover view shows it from Route 114. That road runs five miles south of East Burke.

A map shows peaks seen from Burke's summit. Jay Peak stands 39 miles off at 3,861 feet. Mount Washington rises 35 miles at 6,288 feet. Camel's Hump stands 50 miles at 4,085 feet. Mount Ascutney reaches 80 miles in that view. Basic earth concepts come first in Dodge's plan. Geology's place among the sciences gets weighed. Its twofold reason is use and curiosity, he says. Finding needful minerals serves the first of those. A state survey's park guide teaches walkers to read one green mountain's bones while they climb it.
60804-daddy-jake-the-runaway-and-short-s:
Daddy Jake the Runaway, and Short Stories Told After Dark, is a story book by Joel Chandler Harris, the Uncle Remus author. The Century Company issued it at New York, with Harris's copyright of 1889. The title tale opens on a Georgia plantation in Putnam County one fine September day in 1863. Uncle Jake, the carriage driver, is missing, and the place is in an uproar.

Jake is over fifty, and it is the first time he has gone missing since his mistress was big enough to call him. Around the tale sit shorter pieces: how a witch was caught, how black snake caught the wolf, and why the guineas stay awake. There are tales of the terrapin taught to fly and of the creature with no claws. Harris writes in the voice of his famed storyteller. The book mixes a slave era escape story with animal lore.
61230-the-geology-of-button-bay-state-pa:
The Geology of Button Bay State Park is Harry W Dodge Jr's guide to the rocks and clays of a Vermont park on Lake Champlain. The Vermont Geological Survey issued it in 1962, through the state Department of Forests and Parks. Charles G Doll was state geologist, and Perry H Merrill directed the department.

The park's name is its first lesson. Clay banks along the beach shed concretions of strange imitative forms, many shaped like animals. One common form matches a turned wood button-mold in shape and size, a disc with a hole in the center, flat on one side and rounded on the other. The older name, Button Mould Bay, was shortened to Button Bay. Behind the buttons lies the glacial story: clays laid down as the last ice lobe retreated up the Champlain Valley into Canada.
61433-mammals-of-mount-mckinley-national:
Adolph Murie wrote Mammals of Mount McKinley National Park, Alaska, issued in August 1962. Olaus Murie drew the sketches and Charles J. Ott took the photos. The book first praises the Denali wilds, where plants and beasts live free of human rules. Foxes dig where they will, grizzlies roam, and the wolf hunts as a respected citizen.

Species parts then treat each beast in turn, from grizzly and black bear to caribou, moose, and Dall sheep. Later parts cover wolf, lynx, wolverine, beaver, and the small mouse world. A checklist of park mammals closes the book. Murie stresses that wide bounds and light human touch keep this free life whole.
61953-the-story-of-my-life-and-work:
Booker Washington, head of the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute, told the story of his life and work in a book issued at Cincinnati in 1900. Curry, who worked with the Peabody and Slater funds, wrote the opening praise. The book was sold by subscription only, not in shops.

Curry says no pen can hold a life that has passed into so many other lives. Washington was born a slave and freed by the war, then rose to lead a great school. His words and work, Curry argues, softened bias and gave hope to both races. Pictures by photo print and pen fill the life from birth to fame.
62043-zurk:
Richard Lewis animates a steel giant in Zurk, from the Winter 1941 issue of Planet Stories. The head blurb calls Zurk a huge, part human war machine. His muscles are tubular steel, and his mind is blank and mechanical. Gentle Marene is next when the black space cruiser calls for its youth levy.

Guyard stands in a hidden attic laboratory, his face etched with agony and defeat. He pleads with the steel man to save Marene. Zurk sits expressionless, his electric cell eyes fixed on the small window. Year after year he has sat there, on the moon's Jupiter lit half. Guyard has hurled thought waves at his brain in vain. Two scant weeks are left.
62831-glaciers-and-glaciation-in-glacier:
James Dyson, head of geology and geography at Lafayette College, wrote this booklet on the glaciers of Glacier National Park, sold at thirty-five cents. The Glacier Natural History Association published it with the National Park Service, in a revised 1966 edition reprinted in 1971. The cover shows a survey party on Sperry Glacier. Dyson begins wide: glaciers occur on every continent except Australia, even on equatorial peaks in Africa and on the high mountains of New Guinea.

He then explains the snowline, the level above which more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. In the park the snowline lies above most summits, at more than 10,000 feet. In the Olympic Mountains heavy snow and cloud push it some 6,000 feet lower than anywhere else in the states south of Alaska. Within the park there are fifty to sixty glaciers.
63377-henry-james-at-work:
Theodora Bosanquet, who worked as Henry James's typist, recalled how she came to that post in a memoir of the novelist at work. She set herself to learn a Remington typewriter at once when she heard he needed help. Within an hour she had begun practice. By the interview she could tap out paragraphs of The Ambassadors at fair speed.

James asked her no questions about speed. He trusted a friend's word that she was the right young woman. She found him massive, broader and stronger than she had expected. His face was browned by the Italian sun. She wondered how a stranger in a railway carriage could ever class him.
63519-fossil-forests-of-the-yellowstone-:
The National Park Service issued this guide to the stone forests of Yellowstone in 1928. Hubert Work headed the Interior Department, and Stephen Mather ran the parks. The Government Printing Office made the book at Washington.

A table of the parks at a glance fills the front. Hot Springs, first in 1832, heads it. Yellowstone stands second, vast at 3,348 square miles. More geysers than all the rest of the world together, the table boasts. Boiling springs, mud volcanoes, and petrified forests fill its fame line. The grand canyon of the Yellowstone, great lakes, and fine trout streams stand there too. The booklet then turns to its theme: whole forests turned to stone on the park's hills.
6353-the-prince-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark and Beverly of Graustark, opens this 1914 romance with Mr. and Mrs. Blithers discussing matrimony. Mr. Blithers, fingers in his ears, conquers argument by shutting out opposition, for it is easier to express himself with ears closed than open. His wife talks for two or three minutes, then subsides in despair, for a woman will not talk to a stone wall, and he counts the discussion won.

Two countries discuss marriage, Mr. Blithers goes visiting, and Prince Robin is asked to stand up, with a letter from Maud and a voyage aboard the Jupiter. The prince meets Miss Guile, wireless messages pass through Totten's hands, and R. Schmidt reads them in a luxurious parlour. McCutcheon writes Ruritanian romance with humour, as American bluntness meets Graustark royalty and love must cross rank and ocean.
63631-phone-me-in-central-park:
James McConnell writes a strange love tale in Phone Me in Central Park, from the Fall 1954 issue of Planet Stories. The first line calls for an epitaph for every man, and a grand and special one for Loner Charlie. The tale then turns to Charles in a hotel room.

He lies in a bed next to the most fair woman he has ever seen. A year ago she was beyond his reach, a famed actress and a public idol. He was a nobody with idle hopes. Now he wakes in her swank Manhattan rooms, in the most select hotel in town. The whole thing feels like a dream, good or bad he cannot tell.
63880-george-borrow-the-man-and-his-work:
George Borrow, The Man and His Work is a life of the famed roam writer by Walling. It came out in nineteen eight. Walling had writ a life of a sea dog of Devon past this book. The front list runs past seventeen parts, from a wind on the heath to a last study of the man and his books.

Parts trace a roam youth, years as a press hack, trips to far lands, and the house by a lake where his famed tale was writ. Critics of that tale, a brave girl and her kin, and a book that was not writ all take parts of their own. The close weighs his gypsy lore and marks what set him apart. A guide at the back lists all heads and names.
64014-the-vanderlark:
The Vanderlark is a science fiction tale by M St Clair, first printed in Planet Stories in January 1952. Its opening pages dwell on the strange quality of deep space. On earth, the worst that befalls us falls on our home world. Even the man on a raft floats on water kin to the sea in his veins. In deep space it is very different, the tale says. No tie of kind binds a man to his place there. The horror of the piece grows from that cold fact.

Aboard ship, McFeen brings Alice bad news. The beasts in their cage grow in number at an odd rate. Worse, he has found a hole in the mesh of their cage. The mesh is beryllium, and could not tear, Alice protests. He has also found a spot eaten into the hull, near the cage.
64098-human-work:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote a work of social theory copyrighted in 1904, following her Women and Economics and The Home. Chapter one is introductory, and chapter two treats man as a factor in social evolution. Concept and conduct, then some false concepts, come next. Two chapters take the nature of society, with the social soul and the social body after them.

The nature of work gets two chapters of its own. Specialisation, production, distribution, and consumption structure the book's second half. Gilman argues that work is a social function, not mere toil. Her economics aimed at reform of women's labor and the home. The McClure house published it at New York in May 1904.
64560-how-to-plan-a-library-building-for:
How to Plan a Library Building for Library Work, by Charles C. Soule, appeared in 1912. Soule wrote as number seven in a useful reference series for librarians. A verse prelude sets the tone: build for use, not for show. Taste, thrift, and thorough work guide the whole plan, it urges.

An editor preface vouches for Soule as the top voice on library building. He joined the American Library Association in 1879 and served it long. His 1890 paper won agreement among librarians on building points at last. Nine press letters in 1892 backed librarians against bad building plans in print. The book distills that long fight into firm, plain advice.
64793-h-g-hawker-airman-his-life-and-wor:
Muriel Hawker wrote the life of Harry George Hawker, the airman. The book came out in London in 1922, with a frontispiece and two dozen plates. A foreword by Moore-Brabazon opens the volume.

Muriel Hawker thanks those who helped her sift a mass of detail. The early chapters and the Atlantic flight needed the most care. A naval officer read the flight chapters for their truth. Hawker was famed for bold flights over the sea. The book traces his work, his risks and his fame. It stands as a wife's record of a pioneer of the air. Two dozen plates show the man, his craft and his flights.
65135-jean-craig-in-new-york:
Kay Lyttleton wrote Jean Craig in New York as a Falcon Book for girls, issued by the World Publishing Company in 1948. Jean Craig had moved with her family to Woodhow farm in Connecticut and feared her art lessons were over. A chance then sends her to New York to study and live with her cousin Beth.

The Craigs meet life with gaiety and courage, the cover copy says. Jean finds a stranger, spends Christmas at the Ellis place, and meets Aldo Thomas, an artist from Italy. Chapters bring the art academy, a sculptured head, a fire, and a crisis for Billie. Other Falcon titles include Jean Craig Grows Up and Jean Craig Finds Romance.
65167-the-deeds-carillon-and-carillon-pa:
The Deeds Carillon and Carillon Park tells how Dayton, Ohio, gained a bell tower and a park through the gifts of Colonel Edward Deeds and his wife. Mrs Deeds loved music from her girlhood and played well herself. Hearing the chimes in an old belfry at Bruges, she resolved to give her own town the same gift, so that fine music could reach the whole community.

The tower's 32 bells first rang out in Easter music on Easter Sunday in April 1942. The book traces the carillon from the Middle Ages, when bells grew from a call to prayer into music, and notes that Belgium raised the art highest. It also tells how Mrs Deeds studied bells and searched for a site free of echo and noise. Readers get the story of a civic gift, from one woman's idea to a park for all.
65321-a-pictorial-guide-to-mesa-verde-na:
A Pictorial Guide to Mesa Verde National Park is a photo book of the famed cliff towns of Colorado, by Hall. His text and shots fill the book. Its maps and sketches are by two kin of his house.

Its rights were held by its maker, and the park firm put it out on the ground. The print work was done at San Francisco. Its first plate shows the great Cliff Palace in its rock bay. A photo text then tells how the green table land, for which the park is named, lifts high above the vale by a set count of feet. Fall leaf gilds the slope in its shot. The road in runs past a town of the first set folk, to the gate in the lee of a great peak.
65614-mr-togo-maid-of-all-work:
Wallace Irwin wrote comic letters in the voice of Hashimura Togo, a Japanese servant in America, gathered in a volume of 1913. Togo signs himself, hoping you are the same, yours truly. Chapters treat the vacuum cleaner, the baby, the dressmaker, and a husband's place in the home.

The first letter tells how Togo quit the house of Mrs Bellus of Trenton, who paid $4.50 a week for general housework. She asks if he is an intelligent duster, and whether he has ever cleaned with a vacuum. He pleads that Japanese dusters are more intellectual than turkey dusters, and begs a trial. Paper-bag cooking, fall cleaning, and apartment life in New York fill later letters.
65735-michael-faraday-his-life-and-work:
This life of Michael Faraday stands in the Century Science Series, edited by Sir Henry Roscoe. The line sold at three shillings and sixpence a volume. Mate lives treat Pasteur, Humphry Davy, Darwin, and Dalton.

Faraday, a bookbinder's boy who rose to lead English science, fills this volume. His finds in the laws of force and the motor changed the world. Agnes Clerke wrote the line's Herschels, and Glazebrook its Maxwell, in the same clear dress. Roscoe's set aimed to give each great name a short, true life for common readers. Faraday's tale, of grit, faith, and genius from the humblest start, is its crown.
65994-modern-book-illustrators-and-their:
Modern Book Illustrators and Their Work, edited by C Geoffrey Holme and Ernest G Halton, with text by M C Salaman, was published by The Studio of London in 1914. The Studio was the house of the art annuals and special numbers. A prefatory note thanks the artists and the many publishers who lent work. Each picture is captioned with the book it came from.

The list of artists runs to some forty names. Edmund J Sullivan shows a plate from Sartor Resartus, and R Anning Bell one from Keats. Frank Brangwyn, Eleanor Fortescue Brickdale, and the brothers C E and H M Brock follow. René Bull, Walter Crane, Edmund Dulac, and Jessie M King stand among them. Harry Clarke, then a young Irish artist, gets two pages. The volume is a portrait of British book art at its high Edwardian flowering.
66161-special-detective-ashton-kirk:
John McIntyre wrote this Ashton-Kirk detective tale for the London Library. Heath Robinson and Birch printed it in London in February 1922. Front ads name past Ashton-Kirk books, Investigator and Criminologist among them. Contents open with Scanlon telling peculiar facts to the detective.

Matters at Schwartzberg, a man in a rolling chair, and a hunt follow. Ashton-Kirk first visit to Schwartzberg and much said little mark the tale. Scanlon meets a man with a soft voice in chapter seven. The special detective works by hint and quiet steps here. Pinkerton tales and Gaboriau cases stand in the same London Library list of crime books.
66403-mammoth-hot-springs-area-yellowsto:
Mammoth Hot Springs Area is a visitor pamphlet for Yellowstone National Park. It welcomes the reader to the Mammoth Hot Spring Terraces. The maps in the pamphlet help plan the visit. A driver may take the Upper Terrace Loop road, or drop walkers at the top to hike the boardwalks down. The terraces were officially discovered by a Geological Survey party in 1871. Dr Ferdinand Hayden led that party.

The springs are noted for rapid deposition, sudden shifts, and random waking. The forces of geology here make measurable changes from one day to the next. Hot water is the life of the terraces: without it, growth stops and the stone weathers gray. The total flow has held near five hundred gallons a minute in recent years. The water is seepage from rain and snow falling high on Terrace Mountain.
66920-keeping-down-the-cost-of-your-wood:
Keeping Down the Cost of Your Woodwork is a Curtis Companies booklet, copyrighted in 1923 by their Service Bureau at Clinton, Iowa. Browning and Samuel Rogers supply mottoes about making life fair up to one's means. The booklet argues that fine woodwork no longer needs a costly special order.

Curtis defines its claim carefully: not the cheapest woodwork on the market, but the best value dollar for dollar, since cheaper goods cannot match its quality through and through. Design leads the case, the firm says, with stock millwork redrawn to suit newer furnishings. Trowbridge and Ackerman, New York architects expert in home interiors, produced the present designs. Good design, Curtis adds, costs no more to make than poor design and often uses simpler forms.
67346-the-meccas-of-the-world-the-play-o:
Anne Warwick's The Meccas of the World, the play of modern life in New York, Paris, Vienna, Madrid, and London, was published by John Lane in New York in 1913. Warwick's novels Compensation and The Unknown Woman are priced at a dollar thirty net on the half-title. The frontispiece, an American allegory, shows a climber five hundred feet above his skyscraper, and still climbing.

The book is built as a play in five parts. New York is in rehearsal, Paris the curtain rising, Vienna the children's performance, Madrid the broken-down actor, and London in review, before the critics. Chapter heads run from the cast and matrimony in New York to the great artiste in Paris, and the soul of old Spain in Madrid. The prologue argues that a play earns its name by furnishing a fragment of actual life.
68009-the-last-lady-of-mulberry-a-story-:
The Last Lady of Mulberry: A Story of Italian New York is a novel by Henry Wilton Thomas. D Appleton and Company published it in New York in 1900. Emil Pollak illustrated it. Twenty-four chapters follow Little Italy's fortunes. A goddess scorned opens the tale, and a spot of yellow paint follows. Juno the superb and the first lady build the rivalry.

Armando, the young sculptor of the opening, learned his art in Genoa. His uncle Daniello carved nothing greater than ten-inch Saint Peters. At twenty, Armando judged his life a failure; Daniello's death frees him for America. The New York chapters bring the Casa di Bello and a flutter in the tomato bank. The Banca Tomato fails in chapter fifteen. The last lady is unmasked, then crowned queen of the springtide feast. A partnership in ten-inch St Peters closes the comedy.
6801-beverly-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon sends Beverly Calhoun east of the setting sun, on the road from Balak, through the Ganlook Gates, and inside the castle walls of Graustark. A ragged retinue, an inn of hawk and raven, a royal coach, and three princes fill the early chapters. A visit, a testing of Baldos, and a shot in the darkness lie ahead. Gossip, a rose, and a proposal follow.

Beverly, in service in a Ruritanian court, must navigate love, rank, and intrigue with wit and pluck. McCutcheon writes with the gay, romantic verve of his Graustark tales. Beverly of Graustark is a sparkling, old-style romance of a make-believe kingdom.
68099-malthus-and-his-work:
James Bonar wrote on Malthus and his work for students of political economy. Macmillan and Company issued the book in London in 1885. Bonar, of Balliol College, Oxford, gives the work to Professor Edward Caird. Five books treat the Essay, economics, moral thought, critics, and life.

Malthus stands second in time and honor of three great English writers, Bonar opens. The Essay on Population of 1798 and its growth in 1803 lead the study. Bonar calls him the best-abused man of the age in a famed quote. Readers gain a fair, deep brief for a much-maligned thinker.
68349-frank-reade-jr-with-his-new-steam-:
Frank Reade Jr, With His New Steam Man in Mexico is a dime novel issued in the Frank Reade Library by Frank Tousey of New York. The writer hides behind the name Noname, as the line's custom was. The subtitle promises hot work among the Mexicans, and the first chapter is headed Kidnapped.

Frank Reade the younger is a young inventor of world wide fame, son of a famous inventor before him. His New Steam Man, a machine of wonderful character, stands foremost among his works. The tale opens in Readestown, the town his family founded, where Frank sorts a heap of mail in his study. A letter from a stranger in Laredo, about a mining claim in the Los Pueblos Mountains, sets the adventure rolling.
68836-and-we-sailed-the-mighty-dark:
Frank Belknap Long wrote a complete novelet that ran in Startling Stories in March 1948. The graveyard of old ships opens it. You've seen them, the old ships, the battered and ruined ships, the ships that have made one voyage too many, he cries. Black hulls stretch away for miles into the red sunset.

Such ships can be bought for a song, if you've a song left in you and still want to go adventuring on the rim of the system. Do you know how it feels not to have a song left in you, he asks. Lucky Jim Sanders broke the bank at Callisto City and walked out two days later without a penny. Pete keeps harping on it with awe in his eyes. A ruined gambler, a cheap ship, and deep space make the tale.
68887-bishop-joseph-blount-cheshire-his-:
Lawrence Foushee London, historiographer of the Diocese of North Carolina, wrote a life of Bishop Joseph Blount Cheshire published by the University of North Carolina Press in 1941. A foreword comes from Edwin A Penick, bishop of North Carolina. A frontispiece photograph by Bayard Wootten shows the bishop. It reproduces a portrait in the possession of Miss Sarah Cheshire of Raleigh.

Cheshire led the Episcopal diocese for nearly four decades. London writes as the diocese's own historian. Church biography of this kind preserves sermons, visitations, and building campaigns. The press at Chapel Hill issued many such North Carolina lives. Stefan Salter designed the book.
69019-elements-of-woodwork:
Elements of Woodwork, by Charles King, director of manual training at Eastern High School in Bay City, Michigan, was published by the American Book Company in 1911. It is the first volume of King's Series in Woodwork and Carpentry, written for school shops and beginners. The book begins with the growth of wood itself: the tissues, rays, and grain of trees, and the defects found in lumber.

Later chapters cover lumbering and the varieties of wood, the tools of the bench from planes to grindstones, glue and sandpaper, and finishes such as shellac, wax, oil, and varnish. King teaches by clear steps and many figures. The manual shows the manual-training movement at its height, when schools taught the hand alongside the head.
69499-anne-hyde-duchess-of-york:
Anne Hyde, Duchess of York is a biography by Henslowe, printed at London by Werner Laurie. Henslowe also wrote Duke's Winton, a chronicle of Sedgmoor. Anne Hyde was the first wife of James, Duke of York, afterwards King James the Second. Her father was Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, the famous Chancellor and historian of the Great Rebellion.

Eight chapters tell her life. Parentage comes first: the Hydes of Norbury in Cheshire, celebrated by Camden, could boast long and honourable descent. Youth follows, then James Stuart, the marriage, and the duchess. The fall of Clarendon, her father's ruin, fills its own chapter. The turning point and the end close the book. The biography restores a duchess often treated as a footnote to her husband's reign and her daughters' thrones.
69984-the-mystery-of-central-park:
Nellie Bly wrote this novel, first run in the New York Evening World and printed by G W Dillingham of New York with an 1889 copyright. Bly was known for Ten Days in a Mad House and Six Months in Mexico. Front ads list the novels of Mrs Mary J Holmes, over a million sold, with Gretchen as the new book.

Penelope Howard, a Vassar girl, loves Dick Treadwell, who came to the college courting another and left in love with her. She is in no hurry to wed, though she knows she will never beg for a husband. The young girl on the bench opens the tale, and Penelope sets Dick a hard task. A reporter's fame carries a love tale in the Bly name.
70129-general-washington-s-spies-on-long:
General Washington Spies on Long Island and in New York is a history issued by the Long Island Historical Society. Front matter lists the society officers and directors who stand behind the volume. Footnotes and endnotes in two numbered sets support the text of the study. The subject is the spy rings that served Washington in the Revolution.

Long Island and New York City formed the ground of that secret war in the 1770s. British held New York was the hub the patriot agents watched and reported on. Names, routes, and risks of couriers fill works of this kind for readers. Local history and national war story meet in the society careful record.
70366-antiquities-of-the-mesa-verde-nati:
Antiquities of the Mesa Verde National Park: Spruce-Tree House is Jesse Walter Fewkes's report on the excavation and repair of the great cliff ruin in Colorado. The Smithsonian Institution issued it in Washington in 1909 as Bulletin 41 of the Bureau of American Ethnology, through the Government Printing Office. The letter of transmittal is dated the fourth of January 1909.

Fewkes directed the work under the Secretary of the Interior, and his paper gives the technical archaeology in detail. Spruce-tree House was the largest ruin in the park, and the plates show its ground plan, its kivas, and its rooms and plaza from every side. Decorated food bowls close the illustrations. The bulletin is a founding document of the park's archaeology, recording the ruin as the excavators found and rebuilt it.
71447-great-smoky-mountains-national-par:
The National Park Service issued this 1954 guide under Secretary Douglas McKay and Director Conrad Wirth. The park lies on the crest of the divide between Tennessee and North Carolina. It runs 71 miles along the range, with 36 miles of crest above 5,000 feet and sixteen peaks over 6,000 feet. The blue haze rising from the valleys gives the mountains their name. The guide quotes Arnold Guyot, the first scientist to describe the range from his own observation. He called it the peak region of the whole Appalachian system.

A history section traces the Cherokee homeland, the mountaineer settlers, and the logging railroads that opened the forests after the first world war. The park movement began in 1923; Congress authorized the park on May 22, 1926. The pamphlet gives visitors the park's geology, forests, and plant life. Botanists call the region the cradle of eastern American vegetation.
71682-writers-of-knickerbocker-new-york:
The Writers of Knickerbocker New York, by Hamilton Wright Mabie, is a literary history printed for the Grolier Club of New York in 1912. Only three hundred copies were printed from type and original wood blocks on French hand made paper, with three more on Roman parchment. Stilson engraved the illustrations. A woodcut view runs from Bowling Green to Trinity Church.

New York, Mabie writes, has grown by a process of destruction, becoming metropolitan through successive stages of self effacement. In these days of four million souls, he says, it is not easy to recall the outlines of the old town. That town was satirized by the vivacious young men who wrote the Salmagundi papers. Mabie's book treats Washington Irving and his circle, the Knickerbocker writers who made New York a literary capital. The Grolier Club issued it as a fine printing keepsake.
71904-alcuin-of-york:
Bishop Browne delivered these lectures on Alcuin of York in Bristol Cathedral in 1907 and 1908. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published them at London in 1908. Browne had held a Cambridge chair in art and archaeology before his bishopric. Chapter one sorts the authorship of Alcuin's anonymous life with learned care.

Alcuin studies under Ecgbert and Albert at York, rises to head master, and joins Karl. Later chapters weigh his letters, York's school and library, and Mercian affairs in turn. Offa, a third archbishopric at Lichfield, and a trade treaty fill the middle lectures. Danish ruin at Lindisfarne and Jarrow draws grave letters from Alcuin in exile. A scholar monk binds England to Europe's court.
71934-balloon-observation-and-instructio:
Balloon Observation is a United States Army manual issued by the Division of Military Aeronautics. The Government Printing Office at Washington printed it in August 1918. Its core is a free translation of a French booklet on work in the basket. An added discourse on balloon observation rounds it out.

The pamphlet lays down the general principles and the limits that govern watching from a balloon. Balloon work, it notes, is more than artillery observation alone. The details of cooperation with the guns were issued apart, in staff pamphlets that changed with the system of the day. Some principles, though, do not change. Visibility decides the balloon's worth: in high wind, mist, or cloud, watching is impossible. The manual is a crisp relic of the First World War's captive-balloon arm.
7213-my-life-and-work:
Henry Ford tells his life and work in collaboration with Samuel Crowther, opening with a plain question: what is the idea behind it all? His chapters run from the beginning and what he learned about business through starting the real business. The secret of manufacturing and serving, getting into production, machines and men, and the terror of the machine follow.

Wages, good business, cheap making, money as master or servant, tractors, charity, railroads, and democracy and industry follow, each treated as a practical problem rather than a theory. Ford argues in the voice of a maker who trusts work, thrift, and service over finance. The book reads as a plain-spoken creed of industry.
72327-colonial-days-in-old-new-york:
Colonial Days in Old New York is a social history by Alice Morse Earle, published by Scribner's in 1896. Earle dedicates the book to the Society of Colonial Dames of New York. Her preface owns that the book might better be called Colonial Days in New Netherland. Much of the life described, she says, belongs to the days of Dutch rule.

New Netherland lasted scarce half a century, but Dutch ways, notions, and tongue lingered long after. Dutch names and traits, she writes, remain a force in New York life to her own day. The book opens on the broad harbour as Hendrick Hudson found it. Earle rebuilds the daily life of the Dutch and early English town.
72770-the-plums-of-new-york:
U P Hedrick wrote a great fruit book for the state of New York, printed at Albany in 1911. Three helpers shared the work, and growers across the state sent in their notes. The book forms part two of the farm station report for 1910. It is the third in a set of fruit books from the Geneva station.

Four chapters cover plums that can be eaten, plum growing, the chief kinds, and the lesser kinds. Coloured plates show scores of named plums, from Abundance and Agen to Burbank and Climax. The work rests on long trials at the station and stands as the standard book on American plums of its day.
72807-idylls-of-the-skillet-fork:
Idylls of the Skillet Fork, by Payson Wild, was copyrighted in 1918 in Chicago. The verse tales are set at Skillet Fork Farm on the edge of a district called Egypt, in southern Illinois. A figure named Bill, called the presiding spirit of the farm, stands at the heart of most pieces.

Titles list a bootleg gang, a mocking bird, a possum hunt, drought, war talk, and a pet calf. The first piece praises the Skillet, a crooked creek through gray bottoms whose green, scummy water haunts the speaker's dreams. Dialect verse, jokes, and farm grief mix freely. Wild writes of plain folk with warmth, using their own speech as the music of the book.
73233-the-haunter-of-the-dark:
The Haunter of the Dark is a horror tale by Lovecraft. The story first appeared in Weird Tales in December 1936. Lovecraft dedicates the tale to Robert Bloch. A verse from his poem Nemesis stands at its head. The scene is a deserted church on Federal Hill in Providence, Rhode Island, shunned and feared by all who knew it.

The narrator weighs the death of Robert Blake, a writer and painter drawn to myth and terror. Officials call it lightning or nervous shock, but Blake's diary tells a stranger tale. Blake had come back to the city from Milwaukee, drawn by local tales of the old church. His face at death and the odd state of the church resist plain accounts. The tale is told as a sifting of evidence by those who reject the easy answer.
74866-stories-of-new-york:
It belongs to the Stories from Scribner set. The book holds five works. The first is From Four to Six, a one act play by Annie Eliot. The last two are A Puritan Ingénue by John Wood and Mrs Manstey's View by Edith Wharton.

The play that opens the book is set in a New York drawing room. Esther Van Dyke sits reading and tearing up old letters. She reasons with herself that she may safely ask her old lover Harold Whitney to her afternoon tea. Two hundred other guests will be there, and nothing stronger than tea will be served. An evening party, with stairs and quiet corners, would be another matter. A picnic would be worse still. The book as a whole gives a taste of the short fiction Scribner's then offered its readers.
75028-all-in-the-dark:
Le Fanu's sensation novel, here in Downey's edition of 1898, centers on Gilroyd Hall, an old red-brick house near the village of Saxton. There dwells Miss Dinah Perfect, an old maid of whimsical and despotic temper, with her nephew and adopted heir William Maubray, an orphan of seventeen in the first eleven at Rugby. Their only young companion is little Violet Darkwell, a kinswoman of eleven whom Miss Dinah has made her property for most of the year.

The narrator warns that he has a good deal to say of the aunt, though the story chiefly concerns William. Le Fanu, whose other tales fill the publisher's list, Guy Deverell, The Wyvern Mystery, and The Rose and the Key among them, builds his mysteries on country-house foundations. A lonely child, a tyrannical aunt, and a dependent heir are the pieces here.
75049-the-shadow-on-the-spark:
Edward S Sears writes a murder tale with a science twist, flagged by its editor as a detective story of a different type. A plate shows a hunchback who throws a bundle of spiked papers into a stove as a doctor tends Inspector Craven. The editor warns that circumstantial proof may not always stand one hundred per cent right.

Dr Milton Jarvis comes home on the liner Homeric from a medical congress at Vienna in the year 1926. His closest friend, Jim Craighead, fails to meet him at the pier as he had hoped in vain. Headlines then tell him why: Craighead, a well-known banker, died of shock after an operation, the papers state. An inquest stands called perfunctory in the same black streamer across the front page.
75880-center-pieces-and-lunch-sets-in-cr:
Center Pieces and Lunch Sets in Crochet Work is a pattern book published by Anne Orr of Nashville, Tennessee. The booklet sold for twenty five cents. Instructions for plate one, the cover design, open the text. Six balls of Cordonnet crochet cotton number ten are the materials. A steel crochet needle number eight works the cotton. Small, medium, and large medallions build the centre piece.

Each medallion is spelled out stitch by stitch in short lines. Chains, trebles, and doubles fill rings and scallops row by row. Fifteen doubles to each scallop finish one size of the pattern. A list of Anne Orr publications closes the head. Cross stitch design sets from 1914 and 1915 precede this book. Such booklets carried fancywork patterns to home crocheters by mail.
76377-the-movie-boys-at-seaside-park:
Victor Appleton wrote this boys' story, The Movie Boys at Seaside Park, or The Rival Photo Houses of the Boardwalk, printed at Garden City in 1926. Appleton also wrote of the Movie Boys in the jungle and under fire. Chapter one, Looking for Business, brings three chums to a popular ocean resort that morning.

Frank Durham speaks first: this is just the spot they are looking for, and a good photo playhouse on the boardwalk would pay. His partner Randy Powell agrees, and Pepperill Smith cries that it is the very thing. Their home town, Fairlands, lies a hundred and fifty miles west. Seaside Park holds fewer than three thousand people in winter, and more than ten times that in summer.
76899-the-man-who-saved-new-york:
The Man Who Saved New York is a science fiction story by Ray Cummings. Its premise is given in the first lines. A man's self, or ego, would not stay in his own body, and that, the narrator says, is what saved the city.

The narrator tells the tale as a secret. The newspapers and the radio never mentioned him, or Lisbeth, or Baldy, or even Porky Jenks, whose wandering self is the heart of the affair. The party kept silent, since no one wants to be billed as a candidate for the madhouse. A Green Giant waded in the ocean off Sandy Hook and remains a mystery to the public. Yet without the narrator there would have been no giant at all. He offers the real facts as fiction, which the reader may take or leave. Cummings builds a comic invasion tale on a body-swapping joke.
76984-rocky-fork:
Rocky Fork is a children's novel by Mary Hartwell Catherwood, issued in a new edition by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston in 1911. Frank Merrill illustrated the book. The frontispiece shows the heroine announcing that she is Doctor Garde's little girl.

Thirty chapters follow the child, called Bluebell in many headings, through an Ohio valley town. A geography school, a furnace, churning, and a blackberry patch mark her days. Miss Melissa disapproves of Rocky Fork, and Miss Biggar arrives with possessions. The first railroad train reaches the valley late in the book. The story opens long ago, with morning sun among the tall hills of central Ohio. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
77033-the-sinister-mark:
Lee Thayer wrote The Sinister Mark, a mystery novel dated nineteen twenty-three. Doubleday issued the first edition at Garden City, New York. Thayer gave the book to H W T, in thanks for his final approval.

The tale opens in a dim restaurant, where Mary Blake sits with closed lips. Her companion presses her to speak, and her eyes rest on his face at last. Chapter heads promise an unstamped letter, a viewless room, and a splash of blood. A big trunk, four photographs, and a duplicate key build the puzzle. Peter Clancy, a detective figure in the heads, changes his plans and asks a question. A midnight errand raises the stakes.
77341-beatrice-of-old-york:
Bee Goode of Boston comes to England as a small girl of eleven, sent to live with her grandfather, Colonel Sir John Haslem, at Haslem Towers. Her cousin Vere was meant to meet her, and her arrival in a Dorsetshire town opens Taylor's novel, printed at Toronto in 1929 by the Musson Book Company. Bee grows up between two worlds, England and the Canada she came from, as the War of 1812 draws near.

The story follows Bee and the young Ned through the war years, including the American attack on York on April 27, 1813. Ned loses his good name and must win it back, while Bee's faith in him is tested by Vere and by the war itself. Love, loyalty, and a child's-eye view of a famous fight carry the tale.
77910-in-the-day-s-work:
In the Day's Work is a set of essays on printing by Daniel Berkeley Updike, published by the Harvard University Press in 1924. Updike, founder of the Merrymount Press in Boston, also wrote the standard history of printing types. The book was printed at his own press. A note tells where each paper first appeared.

The contents hold three pieces: On the Planning of Printing, Style in the Use of Type, and The Seven Champions of Typography. The first essay first appeared in The Fleuron, a London journal of fine printing. Updike writes as a master printer on how type should be chosen and set. The essays speak for the craft revival in American printing.
78935-day-s-work:
Day's Work is a science fiction story by Noel Loomis about gods who shape living worlds. It opens with a being striding across the galaxies with feet spanning eons. He aims to make a kind of two legged creature that the council has forbidden. Two gods, Mogar and Dalen, have argued the point all one long morning.

Mogar, ranking member of the council, speaks from the Lesser Magellanic Cloud. His thought rolls ninety light years to Dalen in the constellation Bootes. No fleshly being, Mogar holds, can ever learn to live a useful life. Biped species with opposed thumbs, he says, always destroy themselves in the end. Dalen answers with respect but will not yield his theory to the elder. Council custom lets each god rule his own sphere without disturbing his neighbours.
79160-the-man-in-the-dark:
John Ferguson published The Man in the Dark in 1928, and Collier reprinted it in the Front Page Mysteries series. The printings ran monthly through that year: June, July, August, October. Ferguson was a Scots playwright who had turned to detection.

The book is built in four parts. Book one gives the murder in the house at Ealing. Then come two narratives of Godfrey Chance, a journalist, divided by a statement from Doctor Dunn. The opening is pure London fog: along the Embankment the fog is worse than in the Strand, and a sulphurous, acrid taste thickens on the roof of Kinloch's mouth. The layered statements make a dossier novel, in the years when the detective story was learning to file its evidence and let the reader sit on the jury.
79541-the-mayor-of-new-york:
Gratacap set his novel The Mayor of New York in the year 2000, and called it a romance of days to come. Dillingham of New York copyrighted it in 1910. The tale opens on a steamer in New York harbor at night. Ships' guests watch the shore blaze with a crown of electric light in the air above the cities.

Chapter titles map the plot that follows. A mayor is shown at work and in love, a trial fills two long chapters, and great riots shake the city. The mayor dies, and in the last chapter the Pope comes to America. One picture shows a threat to argue the matter with guns. The book is an early guess at a future New York, full of wonder and alarm at once.
8041-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Mark's Gospel begins at once: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, with John baptising in the wilderness. There is no birth story and no long genealogy. Jesus moves swiftly from baptism to temptation, to preaching in Galilee, healing the sick, calming storms, feeding crowds, and confronting Jerusalem's leaders, until the passion and the empty tomb. The pace is urgent, and the word immediately recurs again and again.

Mark is the shortest Gospel and probably the earliest, prized for its vivid, breathless storytelling. Its Jesus is a man of action, misunderstood even by his disciples, and its ending leaves readers to answer who he is. In the King James Version, its directness makes it the best Gospel for a first, fast reading of Jesus' life.
8071-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-ma:
Alexander Maclaren's expositions on Mark work through the shortest Gospel passage by passage. His titles include What the Gospel Is, The Strong Forerunner and the Stronger Son, Mighty in Word and Deed. Healing and Service, Christ's Touch, Christ's Authority to Forgive, The Publicans' Friend, and The Secret of Gladness. Later sermons cover the anger and grief of Jesus, his ambassadors, and the mistakes of his foes and friends.

Maclaren reads Mark as a Gospel of action, and his sermons match that pace, short and pointed. The volume is useful for anyone preaching or studying Mark, since each exposition stands alone. It shows Victorian preaching at its most practical, turning each miracle and conflict into counsel for daily discipleship.
8268-the-world-english-bible-web-mark:
Mark, in the World English Bible, opens with the beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, Son of God. As written in the prophets: a messenger preparing the way, a voice crying in the wilderness to make the Lord's paths straight. John comes baptising in the wilderness, preaching repentance for forgiveness of sins, and all Judea and Jerusalem go out to him, baptised in the Jordan, confessing sins. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the Gospel moves swiftly to the cross and empty tomb.

The modern version keeps Mark's urgency, with notes on prophetic quotations and on baptism as immersion. Its plain sentences suit a first, fast reading of Jesus' life. For readers new to the Gospels, Mark here offers the shortest, most direct account, in language that never gets in the way.
8564-life-and-travels-of-mungo-park:
Mungo Park's Life and Travels, with a full narrative of subsequent adventure in Central Africa, tells the Scottish explorer's journeys into West Africa. Contents open with an introduction, and illustrations show Park passing a lion, which quietly suffered the party to pass though they were fairly within its reach. Park sought the Niger River and the city of Timbuktu.

Park, a surgeon turned explorer, wrote one of the great travel books, plain and gripping, about African kingdoms, captivity, and survival.
