He died on a second expedition, and later narratives complete his story. Readers get exploration at its most personal, and a book that shaped Europe's image of Africa.
8829-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
R. F. Weymouth's Mark, in the third edition of 1913, opens with the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Isaiah's promise of a messenger preparing the Lord's way. John the Baptizer appears in the desert, proclaiming a baptism of the penitent for forgiveness of sins. People of all classes from Judaea and Jerusalem confess their sins and are baptized in the Jordan. John wears camel's hair and lives roughly, in Mark's brisk manner.

Weymouth's modern speech keeps Mark's pace: short scenes, urgent movement, healings, parables, and conflict with religious leaders, driving toward the Passion. The translation, first published in 1909, favours clarity over majesty, and it suits readers who want Mark's action without archaic diction. This single-book volume lets a reader follow the shortest gospel straight through in Weymouth's plain English.
9571-snow-bound-and-other-poems-part-4-f:
Part four of volume two of Whittier's works leads with Snow-Bound, his beloved winter idyll of the family homestead. The poem recalls his father, mother, brother, sisters, uncle, aunt, and the schoolmaster who boarded with them. Harriet Livermore, the half-welcome guest, adds fire to the fireside scenes. Snow shuts the house in, and tales fill the long nights.

Other poems in the part include My Triumph, In School-Days, My Birthday, and Red Riding-Hood, with A Legacy and Abram Morrison beside. Whittier writes of home with warmth and exact recall. A reader gets his most cherished fireside poem, plus short lyrics of youth and age, in one gathering.
9579-songs-of-labor-and-reform-part-5-fr:
Part five of volume three of Whittier's works gathers his Songs of Labor and Reform. The Quaker of the Olden Time opens, praising a calm, firm man unspotted by his age's wrongs. Democracy, Seed-Time and Harvest, and To the Reformers of England follow. Songs of Labor then salute shoemakers, fishermen, lumbermen, ship-builders, drovers, and huskers in turn.

Later pieces take in a Brussels peace meeting, a prisoner for debt, and the poor voter on election day, with disarmament and Italy's freedom beside. Whittier honors toil and peace with equal warmth. A reader gets reform verse of breadth and heart, where work itself becomes a hymn.
9585-at-sundown-and-other-poems-part-5-f:
Part five of volume four of Whittier's works centers on At Sundown, his late poems of age and memory. At Sundown opens, addressed to a poet friend, with winter grass and arbutus under snow as signs of hope. The Christmas of 1888, The Vow of Washington, and The Captain's Well follow. Tributes to Holmes on his eightieth birthday and to James Russell Lowell add warmth.

Later poems mark Haverhill's 250 years, honor Milton and Sigourney, and watch the wind of March and the last eve of summer. Whittier, old and honored, writes with calm and grace. A reader gets a poet's sundown verse, gentle and luminous, from a life near its close.
a-dark-night-s-work:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens in Hamley, a small county town, where Mr. Wilkins the attorney dines with the gentry his family has served for three generations. His son Edward inherits the practice and the standing, and marries a woman above the family's habits. One dark night, a quarrel in the Wilkins household ends in a killing.

The rest of the novella follows the hiding of that night's work and the long weight it lays on Edward and on Dixon, the loyal servant who shares the secret. A daughter grows up under its shadow. Gaskell, writing in the 1896 collection used here, turns a crime story into a study of guilt eating a respectable life from inside.
a-man-of-mark: Anthony Hope tells of a man of mark in a Ruritanian style romance. Chapters follow the movement and the man, a financial expedient, and an excess of authority. Overtures from the opposition, a mine laid, and Johnny Carr willful deepen the plot. Hope writes of Aureataland, diplomacy, and dividing the spoils.
after-dark:
Wilkie Collins strings his short tales on a single thread in this collection, as his preface explains. The frame is Leah's diary: Leah is the wife of a traveling portrait painter who is losing his sight. While he rests his eyes, friends and sitters tell stories, which Leah writes down to earn money.

The tales between the diary entries run to mystery, crime, and strange adventure, each with its own prologue from the painter. Ghostly warnings, hidden identities, and narrow escapes fill the pages. Collins, a master of suspense, built the frame with real care, so the frame story itself, about art, poverty, and a wife's devotion, holds its own beside the tales.
at-sundown-and-other-poems-part-5-from-v:
John Greenleaf Whittier's late poems form this fifth part of the fourth volume of his collected works. Whittier, the Quaker poet of New England, wrote many of these pieces in his eighties, and the title poem looks toward life's evening. A Christmas dedication poem of 1888 opens the set, addressed to a fellow poet and friend.

Contents range widely: The Vow of Washington, The Captain's Well, and a tribute to Haverhill covering 1640 to 1890. Birthday verses honour Oliver Wendell Holmes at eighty, while other poems memorialise James Russell Lowell and Lydia Sigourney. Burning Drift-Wood gives the set its emblem: an old man feeding his fire with wreckage, thankful that the best remains after loss.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-at-work:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this volume in 1909. Patsy Doyle opens the story at a New York breakfast table, showing her father news that makes him sit up. The nieces then take up work in Kenneth's district, where the Honourable Erastus Hopkins rules local politics and a campaign's returns from Fairview will decide matters.

Kenneth takes a bold step, an artist joins the cause, and a forged check plus a mysterious disappearance darken the fight. Lucy's ghost haunts a backstory of Will Rogers, a disappointed man broken early by lost ambition yet devoted to his wife and child. Patsy eavesdrops, Beth meets a rebuff, and a bubble gets pricked before the awakening. Reform politics and village mystery share the plot.
beeton-s-book-of-needlework:
Isabella Beeton's name fronts this great pattern book, first published in Britain in 1870 and reprinted in facsimile by Chancellor Press. Six hundred engravings illustrate tatting, crochet, knitting, and netting patterns. Embroidery, point lace, guipure d'art, Berlin work, monograms, initials, pillow lace, and lace stitches complete the promise. Every pattern states the exact quantity of material it needs.

Instructions run stitch by stitch, in the imperative mood of the workroom. One crochet round works twenty double crochet into the seventeen chain, then chains and singles in a rhythm the reader repeats from a star. A preface traces needlework from the earliest records to the Victorian parlour. The book served as the needlework companion to Mrs. Beeton's household fame: no ornament a lady might make is left unpatterned.
beverly-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon's Beverly of Graustark is a Ruritanian romance set in the imaginary mountain principality of Graustark, east of the setting sun. The contents promise an inn of the hawk and raven, a castle, a royal coach, three princes, a testing of Baldos, and a boy who disappears.

Beverly Calhoun, the American heroine, travels the road from Balak through the Ganlook Gates and inside the castle walls, amid gossip, proposals, shots in the darkness and a grotto's secrets. McCutcheon writes in the high-spirited, romantic manner that made Graustark famous among readers of light adventure. Anyone who enjoys imaginary kingdoms, dashing princes and plucky heroines will find Beverly pure entertainment.
britannica-1911-aard-vark:
Aard-vark, Dutch for earth-pig, receives a natural history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry covers the mammals of genus Orycteropus, found only in Africa. The Cape form, O capensis, and a northern form from Egypt's side are named as chief kinds.

Stout body, arched back, long ears, and a tail thick at the base mark the beast. A disk snout, small tube mouth, and long tongue suit its trade. By night it tears into ant-hills with strong claws and licks the insects up. One large female ran six feet eight inches over all. Skins bring hunters, and the flesh is salted and smoked for food. Pale sandy hair lies thin on the Cape kind, thinner still on the northern.
britannica-1911-albany-new-york:
Albany is a city in New York, the seat of Albany county and the state capital. It stands on the west bank of the Hudson river, just below the Mohawk. The city lies one hundred forty five miles north of New York City. Its people numbered one hundred thousand two hundred fifty three in nineteen ten. Rail lines, canals, and river steamboats all serve the city as a hub.

Albany sits in a fine setting on hills that rise sharp from the river. The older parts of the city recall Dutch colonial days of settlement. Fine houses in Dutch and later colonial styles still stand there. The Schuyler mansion, built in seventeen sixty, is the most famed of them. The new State Capitol ranks as the finest public building in the city.
britannica-1911-albion-new-york:
Albion, a village in New York state, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county-seat of Orleans county, about thirty miles west-north-west of Rochester, and held about 5,016 people in 1910. The New York Central railway, an electric line, and the Erie Canal all serve it. The village was settled in 1812 and became county-seat in 1825.

Public buildings include the court house, jail, surrogate's office, Swan Library, and a state refuge for women founded in 1890. Mount Albion Cemetery, two miles south-east, is called beautiful in the entry. Albion centres the Medina sandstone industry and ships the produce of a good farming region, especially apples, cabbages, and beans. Its works make farm implements, vinegar, evaporated and canned fruit and vegetables, backed by two large cold-storage houses.
britannica-1911-amsterdam-new-york:
Amsterdam is a city of Montgomery county, New York, standing on the north bank of the Mohawk river about thirty-three miles north-west of Albany. Its population rose from 17,336 in 1890 to 31,267 in 1910, with a large foreign-born share. The New York Central and West Shore railways and the Erie Canal serve it, and hills on both sides of the river command fine views of the Mohawk Valley.

Manufacturing dominates the city's economy. Carpets and rugs lead its factory products, valued at over five million dollars in 1905, and hosiery and knit goods rank Amsterdam third among American cities in that trade. Brushes, brooms, buttons, silk gloves, and electrical supplies follow. Settled about 1775 as Veedersburg, the place took its present name in 1804, became a village in 1830, and was chartered as a city in 1885.
britannica-1911-anne-of-denmark:
Anne of Denmark (1574-1619), queen of James the First of England, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Frederick the Second, king of Denmark and Norway. Born in December 1574, she was married by proxy to King James in August 1589, against the wish of Queen Elizabeth. The match settled the Scottish claims to the Orkney and Shetland islands.

The article tells how a violent storm drove her ship to the coast of Norway on her way to Scotland. Witches in Denmark and Scotland were burned for raising that storm. James came to meet her, and the pair wed in person in November. They reached Scotland in May 1590. Anne was linked to scandals and deeds of force, though the entry says no proof backs the charges. The birth of an heir in 1594 made her place more firm.
britannica-1911-asbury-park:
Asbury Park is a city in Monmouth county in New Jersey on the Atlantic coast. A 1911 Britannica entry charts its jump from 4148 people in 1900 to 10150 in 1910. Two railways and electric lines link it to other shore resorts north and south. Fresh water lakes bound the city and reach back into wooded country.

Summer guests swell the town to near fifty thousand at the high season. A fine beach with a mile long boardwalk draws the crowds each year. The city owns the beach and runs its own water works from deep wells. Hotels and cottages house a large flow of guests in fall and winter too.
britannica-1911-auburn-new-york:
Auburn is a city and the county seat of Cayuga county, New York, south-west of Syracuse on an outlet of Owasco Lake, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. Its people grew from 25,858 in 1890 to 34,668 in 1910. It sits among low hills in the lake country of western New York, with wide streets and many shade trees.

Among its buildings are a city hall, a hospital, orphan homes, and a library, and a bronze statue marks William H Seward, who made his home here. The city holds the Auburn state prison, opened in 1816, and a Presbyterian seminary founded in 1819. It owns its water supply, pumped from Owasco Lake. Its factories made goods worth over thirteen million dollars in 1905, led by farm tools, in which Auburn ranked fifth among the cities of the United States.
britannica-1911-baldwin-james-mark:
James Mark Baldwin (born 1861) was an American philosopher and psychologist, born at Columbia, South Carolina. He studied at Princeton and at several German universities. He taught philosophy at Toronto from 1889, psychology at Princeton from 1893, and then both subjects at Johns Hopkins from 1903.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his honours: a founder of the Psychological Review, president of the American Psychological Association in 1897–1898, and holder of a gold medal from the Danish academy. His books named here include Handbook of Psychology, Story of the Mind, and Mental Development in the Child and the Race. He also edited the Dictionary of Philosophy and Psychology.
britannica-1911-batavia-new-york:
Batavia is a village and the county seat of Genesee county, New York, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on Tonawanda Creek, about thirty-six miles north-east of Buffalo, and is served by three railways. Its people numbered 11,613 in 1910. The town holds the state school for the blind, a Catholic academy, and a museum in the old Holland Land Office of 1804, full of relics of early New York.

Schools and factories fill the rest. In 1898 the head of schools, John Kennedy, began the “Batavia scheme” there. In large classes a second teacher helped slow pupils one by one, side by side with the class teacher. Town works made harvesters, ploughs, and other farm tools, guns, rubber tires, and shoes. Batavia was laid out in 1801, and the famed Morgan affair, a Mason's supposed murder in 1826, began there.
britannica-1911-bench-mark:
Bench-mark is a surveyor’s mark cut in stone or other lasting material. It fixes a known point in a line of levels, from which heights across a district can be measured. The name comes from the angle-iron set into the horizontal cut as a “bench,” a rest for the levelling staff.

A broad-arrow mark is usually cut with the bench-mark, its point sitting on the horizontal bar. That pairing lets later surveyors find the exact spot again and trust its recorded height. The entry is a short technical note: what the mark is, how the staff rests on it, and the sign that guards it. Such marks quietly underpin every careful map of levels.
britannica-1911-brickwork:
Brickwork covers building done with bricks, and the long entry works through the craft from tools to finished walls. First come the bricklayer's kit: a trowel for spreading mortar, a plumb-rule to keep walls upright or at a set lean, a spirit-level and straight-edge for level runs. A gauge-rod marked with the brick courses.

Corners, called quoins, go up first with the rod as guide, and the work between them is kept true by line and line pins set in the joints. Cutting gets close treatment too: hard bricks are scored on a V-shaped block and trimmed with bolster, club-hammer and scutch, a small axe. Soft rubbers and malms are sawn with a frame saw whose blade is soft iron wire. Pointing tools, the hawk and the Frenchman round out the kit list.
britannica-1911-cork:
Cork, the outer bark of the cork oak, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word may come through Spanish from a Latin term for bark. The tree is an evergreen oak growing about thirty feet high. It thrives in southern Europe and on the North African coasts. Spain and Portugal are its chief seats of cultivation.

Fresh layers build the bark, year by year, into a thick, soft mass. That mass can be squeezed and springs back, the trait that gives cork its worth. The first stripping comes when a tree is fifteen to twenty years old. That virgin cork is rough and woody, fit only for tanning or rustic work. Later strippings come every eight or ten years, each finer than the last. Trees bear the process for a hundred and fifty years and more.
britannica-1911-deer-park:
Deer park is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names an enclosure of rough wooded pasture kept for red deer or fallow deer. The entry sets a park apart from a deer forest. A park is always fenced or walled and fairly small in size.

A forest, by contrast, covers a much larger area and is open. Some forests hold almost no trees at all. In old England the right to keep a deer park belonged to the crown alone. No subject could enclose one without a direct grant, called a licence to impark. The entry notes that such parks already existed when Domesday Book was made.
britannica-1911-falkirk:
Falkirk is a burgh in Stirlingshire in Scotland, set out in a 1911 Britannica town entry. Its people rose from under twenty thousand in 1891 to over twenty nine thousand in 1901. High ground gives it a view over the rich Carse of Falkirk below. It sits midway between Edinburgh and Glasgow, south east of Stirling town.

Grangemouth serves as its port, and two canals pass north and south of the burgh. Suburbs such as Camelon and Grahamston now form part of the whole town. The church dates from 1811, though its yard holds graves from two famed battles. Knights who fell in 1298 and officers killed in 1746 rest there side by side.
britannica-1911-hamilton-new-york:
Hamilton is a village of Madison county, New York. Utica lies about 29 miles to the north-east. The village population was 1,689 in 1910. The New York, Ontario & Western railway serves it. A productive farming region surrounds the village. Hops form a large part of its trade. Canned vegetables, lumber and knit goods are manufactured. Valuable stone quarries stand nearby. The village owns its water and electric-light systems.

Colgate University is the village's chief institution. It began in 1819 as a Baptist training school. Its first name was the Hamilton Literary and Theological Institution. Madison University was its chartered name from 1846. Renaming in 1890 honoured the Colgate family of benefactors. In 1908–1909 it taught 307 college students. Its library held 54,000 volumes. The surrounding township was settled about 1790. The village itself incorporated in 1812. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hamilton, New York entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hopkins-mark:
Mark Hopkins (1802-1887) was an American teacher and college head, born in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, as this 1911 Britannica article records. He graduated at Williams College in 1824, tutored there, and after a medical degree became professor of moral philosophy and rhetoric in 1830. He was licensed to preach in 1833.

Hopkins was president of Williams College from 1836 until 1872, and the article calls him one of the ablest of the old type of college president. His lectures on the evidences of Christianity, out in 1846, stayed a favoured textbook for long. Other works cover moral science, the law of love, and the study of man. He also led the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions from 1857 until his death at Williamstown in 1887.
britannica-1911-huntington-new-york:
Huntington is a township of Suffolk county, New York, on the north side of Long Island. Huntington Bay, part of Long Island Sound, bounds it on the north. Its people numbered 10,236 in 1905 and 12,004 in 1910. The south part of the town is given to market gardens. Along the Sound stand villages known for the fine homes of New York business men.

Northport, the most easterly of these villages, had 2,096 people in 1910. It has a large law book house, ship yards, and rich oyster beds. Cold Spring Harbor lies thirty-two miles east of Brooklyn. It was once famed for whale fishing. It is now known for a state fish hatchery and for science labs set up there by Brooklyn and Washington bodies.
britannica-1911-johnstown-new-york:
Johnstown is a city in New York state, and the county seat of Fulton county, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a gazetteer entry. The city stands on Cayadutta Creek, about four miles north of the Mohawk river. It lies about forty eight miles north west of Albany. Its count was 10,130 in 1900 and 10,447 in 1910.

A local railroad and an electric line to Schenectady serve the city. Public buildings named include a Federal building, a city hall, and a Carnegie library of 1902. The most noted building is Johnson Hall, the entry says. Sir William Johnson built that fine old mansion in 1762 and lived there until his death. His grave lies just outside the present church of St John. Two stone forts once flanked the hall, and one of them still stands.
britannica-1911-kesmark:
Késmárk is a town of Hungary in the county of Szepes, 240 miles northeast of Budapest by rail, with 5560 people in 1900. It stands on the Poprad at an altitude of 1950 feet, ringed on all sides by mountains. Its buildings include a Gothic parish church of the 15th century with fine carved altars, a wooden Protestant church of the 17th century, and an old town hall.

About 12 miles west lies the famous watering place Tatrafüred, at the foot of the Schlagendorfer peak in the Tatra Mountains. Késmárk is one of the oldest and most weighty Saxon settlements in the north of Hungary. It became a royal free town at the end of the 13th century. In 1440 it became the seat of the counts of Szepes, and in 1464 King Matthias Corvinus granted it new privileges.
britannica-1911-lanark:
Lanark is a royal burgh and the county town of Lanarkshire, Scotland. The 1911 Britannica article places it on high ground near the right bank of the Clyde, thirty-one miles south-east of Glasgow. Its count in 1901 was 6,440 people. The town draws many holiday guests, since trips to the falls of the Clyde start from there. Its chief buildings include a town hall, county buildings, and three hospitals.

Work in the town covers cotton spinning and weaving, nail making, and oil works, with busy markets for cattle and sheep. Lanark is a place of great age. A parliament sat there in 978, and Scots kings lodged there at times. William Wallace burned the town and slew the English sheriff near the start of his rise. The entry names a gorge, a Roman bridge, and a cave where Wallace hid.
britannica-1911-lemon-mark:
Mark Lemon was the editor of Punch, the famed comic weekly, born in London in the early eighteen hundreds. He had a born gift for press work and the stage. In his mid twenties he quit plain trade work to write plays full time, and a great run of his stage pieces were shown in London.

The 1911 Britannica entry pairs that stage life with press work for a host of papers, and a farm paper he founded. With a partner he thought up Punch, and the two were its first joint editors and part owners. The paper limped at first, and Lemon kept it alive from the gains of his plays. Sold on, it stayed in his hands as sole editor till his death, and won vast reach and sway.
britannica-1911-mark:
Mark is a word whose chief meanings grow, in likely order, from boundary, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces them in a word entry. From a boundary comes an object set up to show a boundary or a place, and from that a sign or token, an impression or a trace. The word appears in all the Teutonic languages, and kindred forms are found beyond them.

In the sense of a boundary tract, mark is obsolete in proper English use, where march has taken its place. It survives, though, for the German mark, a tract of land held in common by a village community, and for old principalities such as the mark of Brandenburg. The Italian marca is also at times rendered as mark. Mark is besides the name of a silver coin of the German empire. That word is a distinct one, at first a measure of weight.
britannica-1911-medina-new-york:
Medina, a village in Orleans County in north west New York, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands on Oak Orchard Creek, near forty miles north east of Buffalo. Its count rose from 4,716 in 1900 to 5,683 in 1910. Rail lines and the Erie Canal serve the village.

Power plants on the creek use its falls and a large storage dam built in 1902. Orchards of apple, peach, and pear ring the town, and beans are a chief crop. Rich quarries near by yield Medina sandstone, a prized stone for building and paving. It is easily shaped and split and was first found here in 1837. The town's growth is traced to the Erie Canal.
britannica-1911-middletown-new-york:
Middletown is a city of Orange county in New York in the United States, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands on the Wallkill river, 67 miles north west of New York City. Its count rose from 11,977 in 1890 to 14,522 in 1900 and 15,313 in 1910. Three rail lines serve it, with an electric line to Goshen, the county seat.

Middletown is situated in an attractive dairy and farming country in its region. It holds a state hospital for the insane, a state armoury, a hospital, and a library. It is primarily a manufacturing city in its work. It has the car shops of one of its railways in its bounds. The value of its factory products rose from 2.15 million dollars in 1900 to 3.36 million in 1905, and the city owns and operates its waterworks.
britannica-1911-mount-vernon-new-york:
Mount Vernon, a city in Westchester County in south east New York, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands on the Bronx River and Eastchester Creek, thirteen miles from Grand Central Station. Its count rose from 10,830 in 1890 to 30,919 in 1910. Rail and street car lines link it to New York City and near towns.

The city is in the main a home suburb of New York, though it has some factories. The township was settled from Connecticut in 1664 under the name Ten Farms. Saint Paul's Church, begun in 1764, served as a British war hospital. Mount Vernon itself was founded in 1851 and made a city in 1892.
britannica-1911-oneida-new-york:
Oneida, a city of Madison county, New York, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on Oneida Creek, about six miles south east of Oneida Lake. The census of 1910 gave it 8,317 people, up from 6,364 in 1900. Railways and the Erie Canal serve the city, which lies on a level site about 440 feet above the sea.

Across the creek lies Oneida Castle, the old gathering place of the Oneida Indians. In the south east of the city is the headquarters of the Oneida Community, which runs large industries here and elsewhere. The city's goods include wagons, cigars, furniture, caskets, silver plated ware, and engines. Chains and animal traps are made nearby by the community. The site of Oneida was bought in 1829 and 1830 by Sands Higinbotham, for whom a city park is named.
britannica-1911-oswald-archbishop-of-yor:
Oswald, archbishop of York, who died in 992, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a nephew of Oda, archbishop of Canterbury. As a young man he bought the headship of the Old Minster at Winchester. Wishing to be a monk, he went to the abbey of Fleury on the Loire.

At Fleury, then a great centre of strict Benedictine life, he stood out for his austerity. He came home in 959 and soon became bishop of Worcester. There he joined the revival of monastic discipline, though with gentler methods than Bishop Aethelwold used. With a great lord of East Anglia he founded the house of Ramsey. In 972 he moved to York, while keeping Worcester as well, and he was buried at Worcester on his death.
britannica-1911-park:
Park is a 1911 Britannica article on the roots and senses of a common word. The word comes through French, Italian, and Spanish forms. Its Old English form, pearroc, links to German words for a fold or a district. In plain use, park has two senses.

First, it is a closed tract of grass-land, planted with trees and shrubs. Such a park wraps around a large country house. Second, it is a like space in or near a town. That park is laid out for show and used by the public for health and play. The term first occurs in English in forest law. There it meant ground closed in and kept for beasts of the chase. Its marks were green leaves, deer, and enclosure. The article shows one word stretching from hunting law to the city green.
britannica-1911-pattison-mark:
Mark Pattison, an English author and rector of Lincoln College, Oxford, who lived from 1813 to 1884, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on 10 October 1813, he was the son of the rector of Hauxwell in Yorkshire. He was privately educated by his father at home in his youth. In 1832 he matriculated at Oriel College, Oxford, in due course.

Pattison took his degree in 1836 with second class honours at Oxford. After other attempts he was elected in 1839 to a fellowship at Lincoln College. At that time he was a Puseyite, greatly under the influence of Newman, for whom he worked. He was ordained priest in 1843 and became tutor of Lincoln College in the same year. There he rapidly made a reputation as a clear and stimulating teacher and as a sympathetic friend of youth.
britannica-1911-plaster-work:
Plaster-work, in building, is the subject of a craft article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Plastering is one of the oldest of the crafts that go with building. The first proof shows that the homes of early man were frames of sticks daubed with mud. A stronger and fairer stuff soon took the place of mud and slime.

The article holds that the mix of plaster was near perfect at a very early date. Some of the oldest work still in place is better in its make-up than the work of today. The pyramids of Egypt hold plaster at least four thousand years old, and it stands hard still. The tools of the plasterer of that age were in shape and use much the same as those of today. For their best work the Egyptians used a plaster of burnt gypsum, like the plaster of Paris of modern times.
britannica-1911-potsdam-new-york:
Potsdam is a village in Saint Lawrence county, New York, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the Raquette river, north east of Watertown. The village count fell a little between nineteen oh five and nineteen ten. The wider township held close to nine thousand folk.

A rail line serves the village, and it has a public library. It is the seat of a state Normal School set up in eighteen sixty nine. A school of technology and a music institute also stand there. The village trades in dairy goods. Nearby quarries yield a famed sandstone, fine grained and very durable. That stone was used for the Parliament house at Quebec and a cathedral at Albany, among other great buildings.
britannica-1911-powell-frederick-york:
Frederick York Powell, an English historian and scholar who lived from 1850 to 1904, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Bloomsbury, London, in January 1850. Much of his childhood was spent in France and Spain. That early life gave him mastery of both tongues and a feel for both peoples.

Powell read law and modern history at Oxford, taking a first class in 1872. He was called to the bar, then returned to teach law at Christ Church. In 1894 he became regius professor of modern history, following Froude. The article grants that he wrote no great single work of history. It praises him instead as a stirring teacher of rare force. His loves ranged widely, from the old sagas of Iceland to modern French verse. Verlaine and Mallarmé lectured at Oxford under his care. He also knew and prized the art of Japan.
britannica-1911-rochester-new-york:
Rochester is a city and county seat of Monroe county, New York, set on the Genesee river seven miles above Lake Ontario. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its growth in numbers: 89,366 people in 1880 and 218,149 by 1910. Many railways serve it, and the Erie Canal crosses the river in the heart of the city on a stone viaduct.

The river cuts a deep gorge through Rochester and drops over three falls, the banks rising as high as 200 feet. Ten bridges join the two halves of the city. East Avenue leads the fine streets, and the park system, planned by Frederick Law Olmsted, covered 1,264 acres in 1908. A statue of Frederick Douglass, who lived here from 1847 to 1870, stands by the main station.
britannica-1911-roger-archbishop-of-york:
Roger, archbishop of York, who died in 1181, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from the household of Archbishop Theobald at Canterbury. There he quarrelled fiercely with Thomas Becket, a fellow future archbishop. He became archdeacon of Canterbury in 1148 and then chaplain to King Stephen.

In October 1154 Roger was consecrated archbishop of York at Westminster. In the great clash between Henry the Second and Becket, he backed the king. The pope made him a legate in England for a time. In June 1170 he crowned the kings young son, in defiance of bans from pope and Becket. For that act he was suspended from office. One charge held that he urged the murder of Becket, but he swore he was clear of it. He stayed loyal to Henry through the rising of 1174.
britannica-1911-russell-william-clark:
William Clark Russell was a British writer of sea tales, born at New York in eighteen forty-four. His father was a man known for famed songs of cheer. He was schooled in England and in France, then went to sea at age thirteen. Eight years in trade ships gave him his store of sea lore.

His first sea tale made his name at once. More tales came in fast flow, one past a plea for good food for sea men. He joined the staff of a news sheet, then a great London sheet as a lead hand. Ill health made him quit that post, though his pen ran on for years more.
britannica-1911-rutherford-mark:
Mark Rutherford was the pen-name of William Hale White, an English author, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and books. He was born at Bedford about 1830, the son of a doorkeeper of the House of Commons who wrote sketches of Parliament for the papers. The son was trained for the Congregational ministry, but his changing views barred that path, and he became a clerk in the admiralty.

He made his name as a novelist with three books said to be edited by Reuben Shapcott. They are The Autobiography of Mark Rutherford of 1881, Mark Rutherford's Deliverance of 1885, and The Revolution in Tanner's Lane of 1887. Under his own name he translated Spinoza's Ethic. Later works listed include Miriam's Schooling, Catherine Furze, Clara Hopgood, and a life of John Bunyan.
britannica-1911-southampton-new-york:
Southampton is a township in Suffolk County, New York, on Long Island. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it between Peconic Bay and the Atlantic Ocean. Bays and ponds lie behind a narrow beach along its south shore. Villages line both shores, with rail links along the south side.

Sailing, sea bathing, and golf drew summer visitors in growing numbers. Fine summer cottages rose near the village from the late eighteen seventies. Locals called the colony the New York Annex at that time. Whale fishing had been a key trade from about 1660. The town was settled in 1640 under a patent from Lord Stirling.
britannica-1911-southwark:
Southwark is a central borough of London, England, bounded north by the river Thames and home to 206,180 people in 1901. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica paints it as poor and crowded, its folk working in riverside wharves, potteries, glassworks, and great breweries. Blackfriars, Southwark, and London bridges join it to the City.

Its cathedral of Saint Saviour was once the church of an Augustinian priory and holds the graves of the poets Gower, Fletcher, and Massinger. The Roman Catholic cathedral of Saint George is a Gothic work by Pugin. Guy's Hospital, founded in 1721, and the Bethlehem Royal Hospital for the insane stand among its charities. The borough is also a bishopric of both churches, made an Anglican see in 1904.
britannica-1911-steenkirk:
Steenkirk, a Belgian village, earns its entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica through one hard fight. The village sits in Hainaut on the river Senne. In the summer of 1692 the allies faced the French near it. William the Third led the allies, fresh from the siege of Namur. The duke of Luxemburg led the French from a strong post.

War craft of that age shunned full, costly pitched fights. A sharp win over part of a foe was the prized aim. William fed the French false news through a caught spy. Before dawn his army moved to strike the French right wing. His lead troops fell on the camps near Steenkirk by surprise. Luxemburg woke to find the blow already landing on his men.
britannica-1911-troy-new-york:
Troy is a city and county seat of Rensselaer county, New York. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the head of tidewater on the east Hudson bank. Albany lies six miles south, and New York City far south of it.

Counts rose from fifty six thousand in eighteen eighty to seventy six thousand in nineteen ten. Three rail lines and interurban electric lines serve the city well today. Troy heads the steamboat route on the Hudson river for north trade. Canals link it with the Great Lakes and with Canada lands. Low lands hold the old town and chief shops and mills district.
britannica-1911-twain-mark:
Mark Twain, the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens (1835-1910), is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Florida in Missouri, he moved as a small child to Hannibal, a town on the Mississippi river. His father died when the boy was twelve, so his schooling was slight. He learned to set type and worked as a travelling printer as far east as New York.

The article tells how he went back to the river at seventeen, set on becoming a steamboat pilot. He later wrote of that training in Life on the Mississippi. The war of 1861 ended the pilot's trade, and he went west with his brother to Nevada. There he began to write for local papers and took the pen name Mark Twain, from a call used when sounding the depth of the river.
britannica-1911-watertown-new-york:
Watertown, a city in Jefferson County, New York, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat, set on the Black River north of Syracuse. The census of 1910 counted 26,730 people there. A single rail line, the New York Central, served the city.

The article lists the chief public buildings and charities of the place. They include the city hall, the county court house, and a state armoury. The Flower Memorial Library held more than twenty-five thousand volumes in 1910. Orphanages, a home for the aged, and two hospitals are named as well. Watertown stood in a rich farming and dairy district and shipped much farm produce. The river gave water power to factories of many kinds. It was settled late in the 1700s and chartered as a city in 1869.
britannica-1911-yellowstone-national-par:
Yellowstone National Park is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the great American park that lies mainly in north west Wyoming. Set aside by the United States as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people, it forms a near rectangle. It runs 62 miles long and 54 wide, some 3,350 square miles in all. Its heart is a rolling volcanic plateau near 8,000 feet high, with the Absaroka range along the east and peaks past 11,000 feet.

The article explains how lava floods in the Tertiary age half filled an older basin and built the plateau. Hot springs and geysers, about a hundred in number, remain as the last signs of the fire below. Old Faithful throws a column of hot water 125 to 150 feet high every 65 to 70 minutes.
britannica-1911-york:
York is the subject of a 1911 Britannica city entry on the old town in Yorkshire, England. The text places it on the river Ouse, where the Foss stream joins it. It notes the town's rail links, its archbishop, and its role as county town. The count given for 1901 is 77,914 people.

Much of the entry deals with the town's past and its built remains. York was a Roman post, and Roman finds are kept at St Mary's Abbey. The walls, in large part from the 1300s, still ring the town. Gates called Bars, churches, and the great church are also described.
carette-of-sark:
John Oxenham set his novel on Sark in the Channel Islands around 1800. His foreword explains the island's forty farm holdings and its feudal customs. Those customs reach back to Norman times, as do its old family names. Carette, of the Carré family, tells the story in the first person, looking back on a youth spent among farmers, sailors, and revenue men.

Sea fights, smuggling, and a feared captor named Torode bring the danger, while island custom and family loyalty shape the choices. Photographs of Sark taken for the book and a map of the holdings in 1800 anchor the tale in a real place. Romance and adventure grow out of a small community that lives by the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-the-:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Park Abbey describes a Norbertine house half a mile south of Louvain. Duke Godfrey Barbatus founded it in 1129. He owned an immense park there and invited the Norbertines to a small church he had built. Walter, Abbot of St. Martin's at Laon, brought a colony of canons and led them for nearly three years.

Once numerous enough, the canons elected Simon of Laon as abbot, and they ministered across the Louvain district, reclaiming those seduced by Tanchelin's errors. In 1137 the abbot founded the Abbey of Our Lady and Sts. Cornelius and Cyprian at Ninove, and Godfrey made Park's abbots his arch-chaplains. Philip, Simon's successor, grew the buildings and readied the soil for farming, while Blessed Rabado's devotion to the Passion marked the house's piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
The old Danish diocese of Aarhus took in Aarhus and Randers provinces, Samso and Tuno islands, and, after 1396, part of Viborg. About 900, King Frode of Jutland raised the Holy Trinity church at Aarhus. Hamburg's Archbishop Adaldag consecrated Reginbrand as missionary bishop in 948, and when Reginbrand died in 988, all Jutland merged into a single diocese centred on Ribe or Viborg.

A fresh division came in 1060, with Christian ordained as Aarhus bishop. Ulfketil, bishop from 1102 to 1134, planned the town, while Svend Udsson, bishop from 1166 to 1191, founded the Cistercian abbey at Om. Peter Vagnsen started Saint Clement's Cathedral in 1201, close to the wooden church Ulfketil had built for Clement's relics. Gifts at Prince Niels's tomb, where he was buried about 1150, helped pay for the stone cathedral, finished about 1263 and largely burned in 1330. Later bishops raised the fine building standing today, and the last Catholic bishop, Ove Bilde, was imprisoned in 1536.

Roskilde stood suffragan to Hamburg from about 991 to 1104, then to Lund until 1536. Its diocese took in Zealand and Moen, with Rugen in Pomerania. About 960 King Harold Bluetooth built a wooden church to the Holy Trinity at his new capital, Roskilde. Its first bishops were Godebald and Gerbrand, both Englishmen, and Aage.

Bishop William began the first stone cathedral. Svend Norbagge finished it in 1080 with King Saint Canute's help and enlarged its chapter to fifteen prebendaries. Svend also completed the Benedictine abbey of Ringsted. Under Arnold, a nobleman led a movement against clerical marriage, and the skull of Pope Saint Lucius I reached the cathedral, whose patron he became. Later glories include the abbeys of Soroe, Ringsted, and Skovkloster, the five-towered church at Kallundborg, and the intact Carmelite priory at Elsinore, home of Paulus Helgesen.

Viborg, in Denmark, covered the province of Viborg, the town of Aalborg, and lands in Aalborg and Randers, the Randers hundreds passing to Aarhus in 1396. The diocese was founded in 1065, after the death of Bishop Vale. Herbert was its first bishop, from 1065 to about 1100, and in 1080 Saint Canute endowed bishopric and chapter, the latter Canons Regular of Saint Augustine.

Bishop Svend I, from 1106 to 1112, drowned in the Elbe at the Count of Stade's hands. Eskild, from 1112 to 1133, began rebuilding the cathedral about 1130. He was murdered during Matins in Saint Margaret's church by order of King Eric Emun. Svend II ruled from 1135 to 1151. Niels I, from 1153 to 1191, gave generously to his chapter. He founded Saint Michael's hospital in 1159 and the Cistercian nunnery of Asmild in 1169. He finished the original Romanesque cathedral, of which only the crypt remains. He secured Kjeld's beatification and the translation of his body to its shrine.

York held metropolitan rule in the north, though its Christian origins are unknown. Bishops sat there from very early times, but the line breaks before the later archbishops. Eborus of York attended Arles in 314. York bishops also attended Nicaea, Sardica, and Ariminum. Pagan Saxons wiped out the early community, leaving only legendary names: Sampson, Pyramus, and Theodicus.

When Gregory sent Augustine to convert the Saxons, he planned archbishoprics at Canterbury and York, each with twelve suffragans, but the plan failed. Paulinus, consecrated in 625, received the pallium in 631, yet held no suffragans. His successors went without the pallium until Egbert in 732. After Paulinus fled in 633, the country fell back into paganism. Celtic bishops from Lindisfarne converted it anew, but York had no bishop again until Wilfrid in 664. The article lists archbishops from Thomas of Bayeux and Thurstan to Walter de Grey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-meinw:
Meinwerk, tenth Bishop of Paderborn, rebuilt his ruined diocese into a center of building, learning, and parish life. Born to the Saxon Immedinger family, he was educated at Halberstadt and Hildesheim. He served as chaplain to Otto III before Henry II named him bishop in 1009 to rescue the impoverished see.

Over twenty-seven years he rebuilt the fire-damaged cathedral, consecrated in 1015. He founded Abdinghof Abbey in 1031 and a collegiate church at Bussdorf. He raised city walls and an episcopal palace, and divided the diocese into parishes. He also revived the cathedral school with teachers of mathematics and astronomy, and improved farming for his people's material welfare, dying in 1036.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cork:
Patrick Sexton's entry covers Cork, Corcagia, Corcagiensis, in Ireland, suffragan of Cashel. Saint Finbarr founded the see and served as its first bishop. Born about the sixth century's middle at Rathculleen, six miles north of Bandon, and educated in Leinster, he spent time on a Gougane Barra island. He then founded a monastery and school at Lough Eirc, the marshy Lee expansion under the city. City and diocese take the name Cork from corcagh, marsh.

The monastery rose on a plateau south of the city, now the Rock, close by the Protestant bishop's palace. Students soon flocked thither, rapidly taking the large marsh island beneath, building there and giving birth to a city now numbering over 70,000. At the Reformation, Bishop Bennett lost the see's temporalities in 1535, and remaining churches passed to Protestants. In 1430, at Cloyne's bishop's instance, Cork and Cloyne united, remaining so until 1747. The 1891 census counted 178,461 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denmark:
A country survey of Denmark as it stood when the encyclopedia was written, covering land, faith, politics, letters, and art. Jutland and islands such as Zealand and Fünen form the kingdom, with the Faroes, Iceland, Greenland, and three West Indian islands attached. Former reach had been far wider, taking in southern Swedish provinces, Schleswig and Holstein, and Norway.

Religious history opens with early missions, including a failed visit by Archbishop Ebbo in 823. Political history starts with ice sheets and ends with a modern state, while literary pages note rune stones, Viking chronicles, and later writers. Art sections trace wooden churches, stone cathedrals, carved altars, and frescoes, with the painter Abildgaard among the artists named.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egbert-archbi:
Egbert was Archbishop of York in the eighth century, dead on 19 November 766, with his birth date unknown. Son of Eata, he was brother of King Eadbert of Northumbria. He was cousin of King Ceolwulf, to whom Bede dedicated his history. He was schooled in a monastery and ordained deacon at Rome with his brother Ecgred. Ecgred died at Rome, and Egbert came home.

Named Bishop of York in 732 on the resignation of Wilfrid II, he took Bede's long letter of advice to heart. Bede urged more priests, prayer and study, the Creed and Lord's Prayer in Saxon, and smaller dioceses for steadier visits. In 735 Egbert won the pallium from Gregory III and became the second Archbishop of York, ruling the northern bishops as suffragans. His pupil Alcuin praised his piety, energy, and gentle sternness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethelbert-arc:
Ethelbert was Archbishop of York, England, date of birth uncertain, dead on 8 November 781 or 782. His name also appears as Albert, Adalberht, and Eadberht. He was teacher and intimate friend of Alcuin, whose poem on York's saints and prelates is the principal source for his life. He was a kinsman of his predecessor Egbert and a pupil in the school Egbert founded at York.

On reaching manhood, he was ordained priest by Egbert and made master of the school. Among his pupils was Alcuin, who described his varied erudition: grammar, rhetoric, law, poetry, astronomy, natural history, and Sacred Scripture. Accounts call him severe to the stubborn and gentle to the docile. His sympathy won his students' affection, and his energy urged them on. Even after Egbert became archbishop, he kept the New Testament lectures, entrusting the Old Testament to Ethelbert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-archbi:
Gerard, Archbishop of York, fought Canterbury for primacy and died disgraced in 1108. Nephew of Walkelin of Winchester and Simon of Ely, he began as precentor at Rouen cathedral and clerk in William Rufus's chapel, which sent him to the pope in 1095. Rewarded with Hereford, he was consecrated by Saint Anselm on June 8, 1096, having been ordained deacon and priest the day before.

Made York's archbishop on Henry I's accession, Gerard claimed equal primacy with Canterbury and refused profession of obedience to Anselm. Sent to Rome over investitures, he claimed private assurances the decrees would sleep, a claim pope and Anselm's monks denied, and he stood excommunicated until confession. He later professed obedience yet asserted York's independence. Reforming York, charged with immorality, avarice, and magic, he died suddenly without sacraments, and canons refused him cathedral burial while crowds stoned his hearse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-mar:
The Gospel of Mark is the Second Gospel, chiefly on Christ's Galilean ministry and the last week at Jerusalem. After a brief introduction on the Precursor, the Baptism, and the temptation, the body covers the public ministry, Passion, Death, and Resurrection. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its contents, authorship, language, text, place and date, purpose, and relation to Matthew and Luke.

Mark passes in silence over the infancy events of the other Synoptists. He cares far more for Christ's acts than his discourses, only two of which run at any length. Miracles are told most graphically and fill almost a fourth of the Gospel, 164 verses out of 677 in the Vulgate. They impress readers from the outset with Christ's power over all nature. The body falls into Galilee, Judea and Peraea with the journey to Jerusalem, and the last week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gurk:
Carinthia's prince-bishopric of Gurk, suffragan of Salzburg, was erected in 1070 with the backing of Alexander II and Henry IV, and its first bishop, Günther von Krapffeld, took office in 1072. Salzburg's archbishop kept appointment, consecration, and investiture at first, the chapter won election rights under Roman I, and a 1535 pact split nomination between sovereign and archbishop.

Grown from a small territory to the whole of Carinthia by 1859, with its residence moved to Klagenfurt in 1787, the diocese counted 369,000 Catholics in 1906 across 345 parishes. Benedictines at St. Paul's, Jesuits, Dominicans, and other orders fill its institutions, its cathedral at Gurk dates to about 1220, and Maria Saal draws 15,000 to 20,000 pilgrims a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesuit-s-bark:
Jesuit's Bark, also called China bark, cinchona, or Peruvian bark, is the famed remedy for malaria drawn from cinchona trees of the western Andes. Its alkaloids made it the most celebrated specific against every form of the fever, and its story shaped pharmacy, botany, medicine, trade, and tropical farming.

Once the bark itself was dosed in many forms; today its alkaloids are made in bulk, chiefly in Germany, from plantations in Java, Ceylon, and farther India. Physicians long praised it above Spanish gold and silver, and Ramazzini likened its advent to gunpowder's for war. Two hundred eighty years of use confirm a drug that changed how fever was fought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-clerk:
John Clerk was a bishop and diplomatist who served Cardinal Wolsey and Henry VIII through the divorce crisis. Educated at Cambridge and Bologna, where he became doctor of laws, he attached himself to Wolsey. He gathered preferments: rector of several parishes, Dean of Windsor, judge in Star Chamber, and Master of the Rolls from 1522 to 1523.

As ambassador to the papal court he presented Henry's book against Luther to the pope before the full consistory and acted as Wolsey's agent in two conclaves. Made Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1523, he was first appointed a counsellor for Queen Katharine in the divorce. He was then persuaded to agree she withdraw from Rome proceedings, and later joined in pronouncing the divorce sentence. His last embassy, explaining Anne of Cleves' divorce in 1540, ended with illness at Dunkirk and death in England in 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-the-moth: Mary, mother of John surnamed Mark, appears in Acts 12:12, where the church gathered in her home. From that fact we may gather she held some wealth, since her house could host the gathering. She may have been a widow, for had her husband lived, his name would likely have been given in place of hers. Beyond this single glimpse, nothing further is known of her life or work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metalwork:
Metalwork in the Church's service covers the vessels and utensils of metal used in liturgy from the earliest days. The practice grew through the Middle Ages, when church metalwork's history was largely the history of metalworking itself. The Church was the foremost patron, nearly all surviving medieval pieces are ecclesiastical, and until the twelfth century monks and clerics made almost all goldsmiths' work.

The entry ranges from antiquity through Byzantine, barbarian, Carolingian and Othonian, Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance work. It centres on precious metals, though iron, bronze, and brass also served the Church richly. Even in the Renaissance, church metalwork stayed a major branch of the goldsmith's art, and today it still ranks among the crafts where that art can most profitably unfold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-york:
The Archdiocese of New York was erected on 8 April 1808 and made archiepiscopal on 19 July 1850. It covers Manhattan, Bronx and Richmond boroughs plus Dutchess, Orange, Putnam, Rockland and York counties, and the Bahama Islands, 4,717 square miles in New York and 4,466 in the Bahamas. The Bahamas joined in 1886, since access was easiest from New York, after belonging to Charleston.

Its suffragans are Albany, Brooklyn, Buffalo, Ogdensburg, Rochester and Syracuse in New York, plus Newark and Trenton in New Jersey. All these formed the original diocese in 1808. Albany and Buffalo split off in 1847, Brooklyn and Newark in 1853. New York is now the largest see in population and most important in influence and prosperity among American ecclesiastical divisions. The entry traces its colonial origins, bishops, parishes and institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newark:
Newark is a diocese created in 1853, suffragan of New York, covering Hudson, Passaic, Bergen, Essex, Union, Morris and Sussex counties in New Jersey, 1,699 square miles. It originally covered the whole state, but fourteen counties left in 1881 to form Trenton. As early as 1672 records show Catholics at Woodbridge and Elizabethtown, East Jersey's capital, visited by Jesuits Harvey and Gage, Governor Dongan's New York chaplains.

Later priests included Alsatians who came with Carteret for salt-making. William Douglass, elected from Bergen, was barred from the first General Assembly at Elizabethtown in 1668 for being Catholic, then arrested and banished to New England as a troublesome person. The colony's atmosphere was intensely anti-Catholic, and the 1698 toleration law expressly excluded Roman worship. West Jersey's Quaker pioneers were more tolerant. The entry follows the diocese's bishops, parishes and growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noah-s-ark:
Noah's Ark, the great box of Genesis, is sized and fitted out in this entry from the biblical text and later reasoning. Three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, it was built of cypress and sealed inside and out with pitch. Inside were three decks of rooms, one small window, and a side door God shut himself.

Trials by modern writers, the entry notes, found such a hull steady for heavy cargo and calm on waves. Inside, Noah's family, pairs of animals, and their food waited out the Flood until the vessel grounded on the mountains of Armenia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-mark:
Mark was consecrated on 18 January 336 and died on 7 October 336. After Sylvester's death he rose to Rome's bishopric. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Priscus. Constantine's letter summoning bishops over the Donatist dispute is addressed to Miltiades and one Mark, evidently a Roman cleric who may be the pope himself. Both his election and death dates are historically certain.

Nothing has come down about any part he played in the East's Arian troubles. An alleged letter to Athanasius counts as a later forgery. Two constitutions bear his name. One gave Ostia's bishop the pallium and ordered that bishop to consecrate Rome's bishop, a privilege Ostia certainly held by the late fourth century, as Augustine attests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-mark:
Mark the Evangelist stands at the centre of this long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It treats the John Mark of Acts as the same man named by Paul and Peter in their letters. Son of Mary of Jerusalem, whose house sheltered the early Church, he carried both a Jewish name, John, and the Roman name Marcus by which readers knew him.

Working through the New Testament evidence, the entry traces his ties to Barnabas, his break and later reunion with Paul, and his close link with Peter in Rome. It then weighs the old tradition that his Gospel preserves Peter's preaching, and surveys what early writers said about his later life and death. Readers looking for the scriptural case, not just the legend, will find it laid out step by step.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-cor:
The School of Cork won wide fame above all in the seventh and eighth centuries. Its name comes from corcagh, a marsh, since Lee floods once covered the low ground where most of modern Cork now stands. Its founder, Barra or Bairre, called Finbarr the Fair-haired, gives the school its story. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a brassworker's son to sainthood.

Barra's family belonged to the Hy Brinin Ratha of Galway's eastern shore. His father, a skilled brassworker, moved to Hy Liathain in west Cork, where the saint was born about the mid-sixth century. His chief teacher MacCuirp, or Curporius, had himself studied under Gregory the Great at Rome. To perfect himself Barra withdrew to a hermitage on a lonely island in the lake still called Gougane Barra, and his school grew from that solitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul of New York began in 1817. Mother Seton sent Sister Rose White, Cecilia O'Conway, and Elizabeth Boyle from Emmitsburg to found a community in New York. The mother-house stands at Mount Saint Vincent on the Hudson. The community must not be confused with an earlier congregation of the same name.

Tension grew over affiliation with the Sisters of Charity in France. Their superiors pressed changes in customs, including withdrawing sisters from boys' asylums, a move that threatened the New York orphanage. At the same time no sisters could be had from Emmitsburg for a much-needed New York hospital, now Saint Vincent's. After correspondence between Archbishop Hughes and Father Deluol, the Holy See extended Emmitsburg's privileges to the New York community on 20 June 1847.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southwark:
Southwark was the diocese covering south London and the south-eastern counties of Kent, Surrey, and Sussex, suffragan to Westminster. This entry dates its founding to the restoration of the hierarchy in England in 1851. When the old London District, once ruled by a vicar apostolic with jurisdiction reaching to North America and the Bahamas, was divided at the Thames.

At first the new diocese also took in Berkshire, Hampshire, and the Channel Islands, and the entry follows its parishes, clergy, and institutions as London grew around it. For readers tracing English Catholic life after emancipation, Southwark's story shows a church rebuilding its organization in the heart of a fast-expanding capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-a:
Paulinus, archbishop of York, brought Christianity to the Northumbrian court and then fled south with its queen. A Roman monk of St Andrew's monastery, he was sent by Gregory the Great in 601 with Mellitus to aid Augustine and carry the pallium. He worked in Kent until 625, when he escorted Ethelburga north to marry the pagan king Edwin.

Consecrated bishop before leaving, he converted Edwin, baptised on 12 April 627, and large numbers of his people. He fixed his see at York, began a stone church, and preached at Yeavering, Catterick, Dewsbury, and Southwell. After Edwin's defeat in 633 he bore the queen and her children safely to Kent. He died at Rochester on 10 October 644.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-of-new-:
New York State, one of Britain's thirteen colonies turned American states, is surveyed here in geography, history, and church life. On 4 July 1776 it adopted the Declaration of Independence with its sister colonies. It spans from 40 degrees 29 minutes to 45 degrees north, and from 71 degrees 51 minutes to 79 degrees 45 minutes west, covering 49,170 square miles, of which 1,550 are water.

Its physical geography runs from the Adirondacks in the north to Catskill and Blue Ridge branches of the Appalachians in the south and east. The article then traces settlement, revolution, growth, government, education, and above all the Catholic Church: dioceses, parishes, schools, colleges, and religious orders. It closes as a reference portrait of a state where Catholic life grew from a persecuted minority to a great communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syracuse-new-:
Syracuse is a New York diocese of seven counties, covering 5,626 square miles, a little over a ninth of the state. Out of 609,041 people, about 161,000, more than a quarter, are Catholics. Its story begins with the Oneida and Onondaga peoples. Their central village on Indian Hill served as seat of government for the League of the Five Nations.

Recollect Franciscans may have said Mass on these shores as early as 1615. Le Moyne the Jesuit counts as the real founder of the local Church. Chaumonot and Dablon said Mass on the chosen site on Sunday 14 November 1654. They raised a bark chapel with Indian help under St John the Baptist. They added St Mary's of Ganantaa for French settlers. Those first missions soon faded, and local histories close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-catholic-:
Catholic gentlemen of New York found fellowship and purpose in the club described here, defined by its constitution as men governed by devotion to the Church and fidelity to the Holy Father. Its objects were to advance Catholic interests, improve members morally, foster a true Catholic spirit, and encourage study of history, literature, science, and art, sustained by a library and frequent social intercourse.

Roots lay in the Xavier Alumni Sodality, organised in 1863 beside the College of Saint Francis Xavier under Father Dealy. In March 1871 members formed the Xavier Union to pursue ends beyond a purely religious body. Clubhouse, membership, and activities follow, sketching educated Catholic society in Gilded Age New York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
San Marcos at Lima is the highest institution of learning in Peru and reputedly the oldest university in the New World. A royal decree of 12 May 1551 had Charles V grant 350 gold dollars to the Dominican priors to found an Estudio General at Lima, with all the prerogatives of Salamanca. Pope Pius V confirmed the decree by a bull dated 25 July 1571.

Until 30 December of that year the school stayed under Dominican control, then became independent with the right to elect its own rector. The first rector chosen was Dr Gaspar de Meneses, a layman. In 1574, after a new site was bought for 600 gold dollars, the name Saint Mark was adopted. The entry follows the university's faculties, colleges, and scholars through colonial and republican times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-york:
In medieval canon law it was received principle that, for judicial matters, sacraments, and the more solemn fasts, the custom of the Roman Church must be followed. Yet for church services each church kept its own traditions, as Gratian's Decretum records. So there arose a number of Uses, the special liturgical customs of a diocese or group of dioceses. In England before the Reformation the south and midlands followed the Sarum Use, while most of the north followed the Use of York.

The general features of these medieval English Uses appear fairly in the peculiarities of the Sarum Rite, which the reader may consult. The entry then sets out York's distinctive traits: its calendar, its chant, and its ceremonial differences from Sarum. It closes with the Use's fate at the Reformation, when the Book of Common Prayer replaced the old diocesan customs across England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-clark:
William Clark was an English priest executed at Winchester in 1603 after tangling with both Jesuits and the crown. His birth date is unknown. He entered Douay College in 1587, moved to the English College at Rome in 1589, took orders, and returned to England in April 1592. In the quarrel over Blackwell as archpriest, he joined thirty-three priests who appealed against Blackwell from Wisbeach Castle in November 1600.

Father Persons attacked the appellants' character, but Clement VIII backed them in October 1602 and restored their faculties, despite efforts to shut Clark out. Found saying Mass in the Clink prison, he faced closer confinement, then arrest over the shadowy Bye Plot. Nothing was proven against him beyond work for Catholic interests, yet he was condemned on 15 November and hanged a fortnight later, protesting his death as martyrdom.
doe-osti-17076746-2026-nde-for-advanced-:
Workshop report ORNL/LTR-2026/4735 records the 2026 meeting on nondestructive evaluation for advanced manufacturing, held May 19 and 20 at Oak Ridge Manufacturing Demonstration Facility. Ryan Meyer, Amir Ziabari, Ryan Spencer, Ahmed Hassen, and Pradeep Ramuhalli organized it. Nondestructive evaluation means inspecting printed parts for flaws without cutting them open.

Researchers, program managers, end users, equipment makers, standards bodies, and regulators took stock of current methods and gaps. Seven technical sessions, a keynote, and sixteen breakout groups fed the program. The report, built from session notes, slides, and recordings, ends with a shared synthesis of themes, top challenges, and research priorities for qualifying printed parts.
doe-osti-2998877-summary-of-the-1st-reac:
Gustavo Nobre, David Brown, Benjamin Wang and fellow participants wrote Brookhaven National Laboratory report BNL-229060-2025-INRE, summarising the first Reactor Graphite Workshop. The meeting ran 8-9 July 2025 at Brookhaven and was organised by the Cross Section Evaluation Working Group. Graphite slows neutrons and forms structures inside several advanced reactor designs, so its nuclear data must be sound.

Talks covered how neutrons scatter off graphite, how radiation damage changes its atomic vibrations, and which measurements exist for checking computer libraries. Gaps stood out: data cover only a limited span of temperatures, and more is needed for firm uncertainty work. Participants aimed to agree on data sets for validation and to shape advice for the next ENDF/B nuclear data release. Training needs and follow-on workshops also feature. The report closes with findings on irradiated graphite, whose main vibration patterns survive damage well.
doe-osti-3002138-unrolled-video-super-re:
Haley Duba-Sullivan, Emma J. Reid, Charles A. Bouman, and Gregery T. Buzzard present a video method in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4188, dated September 2025. Their method sharpens low-resolution video, a task called super-resolution. It applies when the motion between frames is already known, as with a tracked camera path. Clean, sharp video matters for surveillance review and remote inspection.

The design unrolls an iterative math method into a neural network, layer by layer. An autoregressive prior adds a learned guess of each frame based on the frames before it. Mixing model-based steps with learned parts aims for sharper frames with fewer artifacts. The report tests the network and compares its output with other approaches. The work targets video tools that must stay trustworthy, not just look sharp.
doe-osti-3013549-fair-data-and-interpret:
Lynda Catherine Brinson of Duke University wrote this final report for award DE-SC0021358. Cynthia Rudin and Chiara Daraio of Caltech served as co-investigators. The report covers September 2020 to September 2025. The project built a FAIR data and interpretable AI framework for architectured metamaterials. These engineered structures steer sound and vibration in ways plain materials cannot. Interpretable means the AI shows which patterns drive performance. It does not hide its logic.

A hierarchical design method stacks patterns at different scales. One material can thus block vibrations across several frequency ranges at once. Uncertainty tools account for defects from manufacturing. They cut physical testing needs by orders of magnitude. Printed samples confirmed the designs in wave experiments. The datasets went into the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository as benchmarks.
doe-osti-3014654-united-states-nuclear-d:
Brookhaven report BNL-229184-2025-INRE, dated December 2025, is the United States Nuclear Data Program's work plan for fiscal year 2026, the year beginning October 1, 2025. David Brown leads the author list, with Lee Bernstein, Jun Chen, and program members across nine institutions. Where the annual report looks backward, this volume commits the program to specific tasks and deliverables for the coming year.

Operations tasks cover management, the NNDC library's re-establishment after its move to Building 490, and customer services. Technical tasks queue new B(E2) and double-beta decay data compilation, XUNDL database reviews with journal author follow-up, and evaluation support coding. Funding history since 2002 is charted. Program staff use the plan to coordinate structure and reaction data work across the member laboratories.
doe-osti-3017719-wireless-high-temperatu:
Xuejun Lu and Xingwei Wang of the University of Massachusetts Lowell wrote this final technical report for award DE-FE0031895, dated February 10, 2026. Dongsheng Li was the industry partner. Total project costs were 432,206 dollars, all federal share. The project built a wireless high-temperature sensor network for smart boiler systems, where wiring sensors into hot zones is costly and failure-prone.

Activities covered sensor designs and a family of Lamb wave filters at 300 megahertz, 900 megahertz, and 2.4 gigahertz. For the sensing antennas the team settled on a commercial high-temperature circuit board material after trials. Temperature sensing at the hot end used 4H-silicon carbide semiconductor devices, chosen because ordinary silicon electronics quit at boiler temperatures. Fabricated 2.4 gigahertz patch antennas are shown with dimensions. Plant operators get a path to dense temperature monitoring inside equipment that used to run unmeasured.
doe-osti-3029848-fair-data-and-interpret:
Chiara Daraio of the California Institute of Technology led this joint project with L. Catherine Brinson and Cynthia Rudin of Duke University, under awards DE-SC0021253 and DE-SC0021358. The subject is architectured metamaterials, solids whose inner pattern, not just their chemistry, sets how they act. The team built open benchmark datasets that meet the FAIR tests: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. They also built a learning system meant to be read, not just run.

That system, Learning Refined Compositional Rules, pulls plain rules that link a pattern shape to bulk sound behavior across size scales. Such rules replace hunches and black-box searches that were hard to reuse. Tests with real samples checked the rules, which now guide tuning of wave spread and vibration control in acoustic devices.
doe-osti-3155999-a-data-driven-phytotech:
Bahareh Nojabaei of Virginia Tech led this April 2026 final report under grant DE-FE0032184, with Hosein Foroutan, Hoda Eldardiry, and Ryan Stewart. Coal ash ponds and landfills at power plants can leak metals into soil and groundwater. The team asked whether satellite eyes plus plant-based cleanup, called phytotechnology, could find and treat that harm cheaply. Phase I work fused old and new Sentinel-2 satellite images with groundwater data at ash sites in North Carolina and Virginia.

Stressed plants betray leaking metals such as arsenic, cadmium, cobalt, lead, and lithium. Random Forest models sorted stressed from healthy growth with high accuracy across sites, and methods that need no labeled field data also showed promise. The result is a low-cost early warning layer for ash sites, ready to guide ground crews.
doe-osti-3376478-triggerable-adhesives-w:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4565, dated February 2026, is the final report for user project NN-24-1485 at the lab's Manufacturing Demonstration Facility. Steven Bullock and Nadim Hmeidat wrote it. The industry partner was Perseus Materials of Knoxville, Tennessee. The topic is glue with an odd pair of traits: it stays workable as long as the crew needs, then sets hard on a trigger. Big composite parts, such as wind turbine blades, are the target use.

Standard glues start to cure the moment they are mixed. That clock forces haste and waste on large-area jobs. A triggerable mix removes the clock. Crews can spread and fit, then fire the set on cue. The report frames the gain boldly: parts faster to make, easier to join, and strong at scale. Sections cover the test results and the patent ground the work opened.
doe-osti-3991171-dst-forecasting-status-:
Dave Osthus and Brian Larsen of Los Alamos National Laboratory give a frank account of a failed forecast project in report LA-UR-26-28531, issued September 23, 2026. Their goal was to predict the Dst index, a measure of geomagnetic storms, from one to twelve hours ahead. Storm forecasts help satellite and power grid operators brace for trouble.

The summary states the miss at once: the team did not reach the goal. Tests showed the block was not the model shape but the data at hand. When the model was fed the true future solar wind as a cheat, scores jumped, but those drivers cannot be known in real time. Watching the Sun's drivers from closer in would help most. A study of sudden storm starts, sharp jumps in the index, rounds out the report as a possible early warning sign.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-mark:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on St. Mark moves at the Gospel's own brisk pace. Alexander Maclaren opens with What 'The Gospel' Is from Mark I. The Strong Forerunner and the Stronger Son follows. Mighty in Word and Deed treats the first healings at Capernaum.

Christ's Touch and Christ's Authority to Forgive come next in the contents. The Publicans' Friend and The Secret of Gladness treat chapter II. Four Soils for One Seed expounds the sower parable in chapter IV. The Storm Stilled and The Lord of Demons follow. Talitha Cumi and The Power of Feeble Faith use the Jairus story. Herod as A Startled Conscience opens chapter VI. Maclaren keeps each sermon tight and vivid.
govdocs-archive_org-man-and-technics-osw:
Oswald Spengler, author of The Decline of the West, published Man and Technics in 1931 as a short contribution to a philosophy of life. Its subject is technology, which Spengler treats not as a neutral tool but as the driving tactic of human existence.

He argues that technics began with the predator's way of life. It reached its peak in Faustian Western man, whose machine culture he expects to turn destructive and to spread beyond its makers' control. The book compresses Spengler's dark view of history into a few chapters. It remains his most read short work on the machine age.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIFeltWMark_FB: W. Mark Felt, once a senior FBI official, appeared on the CBS News program Face the Nation on August 29, 1976. The archived record preserves that broadcast appearance under his name. The file gives the program, the network, and the date. It gives no transcript detail in the surviving evidence. It stands as a dated record of Felt answering questions in public during the post-Watergate years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeissMark_Weiss: Harold Weisberg wrote on April 28, 1983, to Barger, Aschkenasy, and Weiss about his FBI Freedom of Information lawsuits. The recipients were acoustics researchers tied to the evidence in his cases. Weisberg's suits forced many assassination files into the open. The letter shows the legal fight and the science working side by side, with experts and a litigant sharing one long campaign.
graustark:
