George Barr McCutcheon's Graustark begins on an east-bound express from Denver. Grenfall Lorry, a rich young American who has hunted and fished on four continents, boards with the air of a martyr. A lady in the dark passageway changes the journey in one meeting of eyes. The train carries them toward a ship, and toward her secret.

The lady is the Princess Yetive of Graustark, a tiny principality in the eastern European mountains. Lorry follows her home, where a forced marriage to a neighbouring prince threatens her throne. Disguises, a prison cell, and a midnight rescue fill the Ruritanian plot. McCutcheon invented the pattern that a hundred romances copied: American pluck against Balkan intrigue. Graustark's success founded a series and a genre. Its princess, its mountains, and its cheerful impossibility still define the imaginary kingdom novel.
jesus-of-nazareth-a-biography-by-john-ma:
John Mark is named as author of Jesus of Nazareth, a biography, published by Appleton at New York in 1922. Contents hail the Galilean and call him a teacher with authority. Thou art the Christ and Strong Son of God are later chapter heads. Crucified, dead and buried, then risen, close the sixteen chapters.

The text follows Mark's Gospel closely from its first lines. John baptizing in the wilderness opens the narrative in the Gospel's own words. Greatness through service is taught on the road to Jericho in a middle passage. Whoever will be chiefest shall be servant of all, Jesus says there.
life-and-travels-of-mungo-park:
Mungo Park's travels in Africa anchor this combined life and narrative. Contents begin with what ancients and Arabs knew of the continent. Park trained as a surgeon before the African Association engaged him. His preparations and departure from the Gambia River follow.

Park reached Pisania, the British factory on the river. Sickness struck him there before he set out for the interior. Later chapters promise a full narrative of subsequent central African adventure. The book preserves the record of a famed early African explorer. Ledyard, Lucas, and Houghton precede Park among Africa's English explorers. Portuguese and English discoveries frame the introduction's survey.
making-both-ends-meet-the-income-and-out:
Making Both Ends Meet studies how New York working girls lived on their wages. Sue Ainslie Clark and Edith Wyatt wrote it for Macmillan in 1911. A photograph by Lewis Hine faces the title page. The authors dedicated the book to Florence Kelley, the reform leader.

The study grew from the Consumers' League's work on laundry labor. Laundry owners met the League to seek a ten-hour day. Clark and Wyatt record real budgets, rents, food, and carfare. Girl after girl tells how her pay falls short of her needs. The book became a classic of Progressive Era reform. It lets working women speak in their own figures.
medoline-selwyn-s-work:
Mrs. J. J. Colter wrote Medoline Selwyn's Work, held in rights in Boston in 1889. Ira Bradley and Company printed the book. A verse at the front urges readers to seize the golden hour.

Mrs. Blake and Oaklands open the tale, and Esmerelda comes third. A funeral, a new skill, and Mr. Winthrop mark the early turns. City life, humble charities, and a Christmas tree fill the middle. Mrs. Le Grande's tale and a changed heart lead toward the close. A helping hand and a pleasant surprise lift the later heads. The tale ends from the depths, after much loss and change.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-1-:
Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward edited this first volume of their father's further letters. Its subtitle calls it a record of his work in hitherto unpublished letters. The editors dedicate it to Sir Joseph Hooker, Darwin's lifelong friend. A quotation from Darwin thanks Hooker for constant kindness and encouragement.

The preface explains that the Life and Letters of 1887 left much unused. New letters arrived from correspondents including Galton, Huxley, Lyell, and Owen. The Hooker correspondence forms the chief treasure, written with complete freedom. Even Darwin's most technical letters gain personal charm there, the editors say, and this volume begins that record.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-2-:
Volume Two continues the letters of Charles Darwin edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward. The biographical footnotes for both volumes are gathered at this volume's end. Its opening chapter treats geographical distribution from 1843 to 1882. The letters here run from 1867 onward.

Letter 378 is from Joseph Hooker at Kew, dated January 20, 1867. Island plants and animals, and how species spread, dominate the science of these pages. Darwin argues distribution is key evidence for evolution by natural selection. Readers watch him test the theory against facts from his botanist friend's global network, year by year, in his modest and careful voice.
my-life-and-work:
Henry Ford tells his own life and work with help from Samuel Crowther. The contents open with a bold question: what is the idea? Early chapters trace his beginnings and what he learned about business. Then comes the secret of manufacturing and serving.

Later chapters treat wages, machines and men, and cheap goods. Ford asks why not always have good business, and why be poor. Money, he argues, must be a servant, not a master. Tractors, railroads, and charity all get his plain views. V1 called it a bestseller that put his creed on record, for better and for worse.
nasa-tm-19710001808-manned-space-flight-:
NASA published this account of its Manned Space Flight Network, the chain that tracked Apollo flights. Tracking, command, and talk with the crews were Apollo's vital links with Earth. The network worked in two broad phases for each mission.

Near Earth, a worldwide chain of stations with mid-size antennas did the work. Once a craft passed ten thousand miles out, much larger antennas took over for their power and precision. The network held a dozen ground stations, one ship, and four jet aircraft. All were linked to the Mission Control Center in Houston. It had to give instant, reliable contact from liftoff to splashdown.
new-york: New York is a work by James Fenimore Cooper, the American novelist. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the work itself. The record gives no year, and the bare title names only the place. Nothing in the sample shows whether the piece is tale, sketch, or history. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only, and check the full text for the work's true form.
podcast-joerogan-7HoFQdKD9Rk:
Paranormal creators Sam and Colby join the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1922. The pair built a huge online following by spending nights in haunted houses and filming what happens. Rogan, a skeptic with a soft spot for ghost stories, gives them the floor.

They trade their best ghost-hunting stories, from famous haunted sites to nights that scared them off a location. Rogan asks how they rule out tricks and what they truly believe they caught. The episode is a storyteller's session: part travel log of America's spookiest places, part debate over whether anything out there answers back.
podcast-joerogan-yUsJIcqwARk:
German author Norman Ohler brings his book Blitzed to episode 2183 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Ohler researched how deeply Nazi Germany ran on drugs, from soldiers' meth to Hitler's own injections. His work changed how many readers picture the Third Reich.

Ohler explains how the stimulant Pervitin fueled the early blitzkrieg campaigns. He describes the drug culture around Hitler and his personal doctor's cocktail of shots. Rogan asks how much the highs and crashes shaped decisions that killed millions. History's dark students get a gripping, well-sourced tour of the Wehrmacht's hidden fuel.
religion-in-earnest-a-memorial-of-mrs-ma:
John Lyth wrote this memorial of his mother, Mary Lyth of York, in 1861, and signed his preface from Stetten in Württemberg. He calls the work an act of Christian duty, not of family affection alone. Her steady example and her prayers, he says, taught him as a child that religion is the one business of life.

Lyth warns that readers seeking startling incident or fine writing will find little here. His mother made no claim to learning and her story held no romance. What he offers is the growth of grace in a plain life, and proof of how much decision, plain purpose, and steady conduct can do.
snow-bound-and-other-poems-part-4-from-v:
Poems by John Greenleaf Whittier fill one part of a larger set, sorted here under nature poems, poems of self and memory, and religious poems. The contents list Snow-Bound first, then My Triumph, In School-Days, My Birthday, and Red Riding-Hood. Later heads name Response, At Eventide, Voyage of the Jettie, and My Trust, with an autograph poem and A Legacy in the next group.

Whittier gives Snow-Bound, a winter idyl, to the memory of the home it describes. His note names the folk of the Whittier homestead: father, mother, brother, two sisters, an uncle and aunt, and the district school-master who boarded with them. The half-feared, half-welcome guest, he explains, was Harriet Livermore, a young woman of fine gifts, strong temper, and fervent faith.
songs-of-labor-and-reform-part-5-from-vo: John Greenleaf Whittier's anti-slavery poems stand under the head Songs of Labor and Reform in one part of his works. The contents lead with The Quaker of the Olden Time, Democracy, and The Gallows, then Seed-Time and Harvest and To the Reformers of England. A songs-of-labor group names the shoemakers, the fishermen, the lumbermen, the ship-builders, the drovers, and the huskers, each trade given its own poem.
the-balkans-a-history-of-bulgaria-serbia:
Nevill Forbes, Arnold J. Toynbee, D. Mitrany, and D. G. Hogarth shared the writing of a history covering Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, Rumania, and Turkey. Contents assign Greece to Toynbee, Rumania to Mitrany, and Turkey to Hogarth. An ethnological map of the Balkan Peninsula is listed.

Serbian chapters run from foreign rule in 650 to the Balkan Wars of 1908 to 1913, through empire, Turkish rule, and liberation under Kara-George. Greek chapters move from ancient to modern Greece and the building of a state. Turkish chapters trace rise, shrinkage, revival, revolution, and a final look at the future.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-41-mar:
Mark in the authorised King James wording, opens as the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. A prophecy is quoted at once: a messenger is sent before his face to prepare the way.

A voice cries in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord and make his paths straight. John baptizes there, preaching repentance for the remission of sins. All Judaea and Jerusalem go out to him and are baptized in the Jordan, confessing sins. John wears camel's hair and a skin girdle and eats locusts and wild honey. He announces one mightier than himself.
the-bow-of-orange-ribbon-a-romance-of-ne: Amelia E. Barr wrote The Bow of Orange Ribbon: A Romance of New York, put out in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company with rights dated 1886 and 1893. Theo. Hampe drew the plates. She gave the book, by leave, to the Holland Society of New York. The plate list names a girl going down steps with a man, a May scene in New York one hundred and twenty-one years past, and a man named Joris Van Heemskirk.
the-cruise-of-the-noah-s-ark: David Cory, author of the Little Jack Rabbit series, wrote The Cruise of the Noah's Ark for the Little Journeys to Happy Land books. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York under a 1922 copyright. A series page names two companion volumes by Cory, The Magic Soap-Bubble and The Iceberg Express. The frontispiece shows Mr. Jonah leaving the whale for the ark. Only the title pages and series matter are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-cruise-of-the-snark: Jack London's The Cruise of the Snark, issued by Mills and Boon with Macmillan holding copyright, is dedicated to Charmian, the mate of the Snark. London praises her for taking the wheel night or day, in and out of port, and in every emergency. He praises her too for weeping when the voyage was given up after two years. Chapters follow on the first landfall, a royal sport, the lepers of Molokai, and the house of the sun. Only the front matter and contents start are present here.
the-danger-mark: Robert W. Chambers wrote The Danger Mark, dated 1909 with pictures by A. B. Wenzell and dedicated to his friend John Carrington Yates. Its contents list ten chapters: The Seagraves, In Trust, The Threshold, The Year of Discretion, Roya-Neh, Adrift, Together, An Afterglow, Confession, and Dusk. A frontispiece caption reads, Please do tell me somebody is scandalised. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-day-s-work:
Rudyard Kipling's story set The Day's Work lists tales such as The Bridge-Builders, A Walking Delegate, and The Ship That Found Herself. The Tomb of His Ancestors, William the Conqueror, The Maltese Cat, and The Brushwood Boy follow. The first story follows Findlayson of the Public Works Department, who expects at least a C. I. E. for three years of heat, cold, danger, and disease spent raising the great Kashi Bridge over the Ganges.

In under three months the Viceroy is to open the bridge, an archbishop will bless it, and the first trainload of soldiers will cross. Findlayson sits in his trolley above the works: a lattice-girder bridge on his own truss, carried by twenty-seven brick piers sunk eighty feet below the shifting sand. A railway runs above, with a cart-road flanked by footpaths. Red brick towers at either end are loopholed for musketry.
the-definite-object-a-romance-of-new-yor: Jeffery Farnol, author of The Broad Highway and The Amateur Gentleman, subtitled The Definite Object a romance of New York, dated 1917. The chapter headings tell a story in themselves: a mournful millionaire lacks an object, Geoffrey Ravenslee goes seeking one, comes to Hell's Kitchen at peep of day, takes lodgings with Mrs. Trapes despite her elbows, and is taught the gentle art of shopping by Spike. Only the title page and the first fifteen chapter headings are present here.
the-explorers-of-australia-and-their-lif:
Ernest Favenc wrote The Explorers of Australia and Their Life-Work, dated 1908, for The Makers of Australasia set. Front pages list kin volumes: Captain Cook and his predecessors, Governor Phillip and his successors, Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and Sir George Grey. A portrait shows Captain Charles Sturt at about fifty-four, from Crossland's painting.

Favenc, himself an explorer and historian of Australian exploration, tells how Cook, Sturt, Eyre, Leichhardt, and others crossed a harsh continent. His preface frames the book as a tribute to those men. Their labour mapped a continent that maps had left blank.
the-lion-of-saint-mark: G. A. Henty wrote his story of Venice in the fourteenth century, first published in 1897 according to the record heading. Only a preface heading and a chapter list are present here, naming seventeen chapters from Venice and a conspiracy through pirate attacks, the battle of Pola, and an ungrateful republic. That count clashes with the companion record of this title, whose list runs to twenty chapters and whose preface appears in full. The tale itself cannot be seen in this record.
the-parish-clerk: P. H. Ditchfield wrote The Parish Clerk, first published in 1907, with thirty-one illustrations. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents run to fifteen chapters. They open with Old-Time Choirs and Parsons and the antiquity of the clerk's office. The medieval clerk, his duties of reading and singing, and the clerk in literature follow. Smuggling clerks, the clerk in epitaph, and the Worshipful Company of Parish Clerks complete the survey.
the-prince-of-graustark: George Barr McCutcheon's The Prince of Graustark, dated 1914, carries illustrations by A. I. Keller. McCutcheon is named as author of Graustark and Beverly of Graustark. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents, so the novel itself is not on view. Opening chapters set Mr. and Mrs. Blithers discussing matrimony, and two countries discussing marriage. Mr. Blithers goes visiting, and a chapter is called Protecting the Blood. Prince Robin is asked to stand up, then meets Mr. Blithers and Miss Guile aboard the Jupiter.
the-red-thumb-mark: R. Austin Freeman builds a forensic mystery around a thumb print. Chapters move from a learned brother to a suspect. A lady enters the case, and confidences follow. A thumbograph device appears before committal for trial. Later headings promise shoals and quicksands. A suspicious accident and a prisoner come next. An assistant named Polton is mystified. An ambush and murder by post close the list. Only the title and chapter list are present here. The case itself does not appear.
the-song-of-the-lark: Cather's 1915 Song of the Lark follows singer Thea Kronborg from Colorado to fame. Art demands all. The Tower library holds the full text. It sang ambition. Plains raised. Voice soared. Art won. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-unspeakable-perk:
Samuel Hopkins Adams opens his novel on a mountainside above the Caribbean Sea. A young American sits in a niche of rock hating the blue water in front of him. He comes daily to the shade and the cool trickle from a crevice, wishing the ocean dry so he can walk home to the United States.

Above him, unknown, a girl rests on the crest of his rock loving the same view. She has just found the private trail, and the sea delights her because it separates her from America and its complications. Chapter titles ahead promise forked tongues, a black warning, a yellow flag, and a woman at a quinta, mixing romance with intrigue.
the-world-english-bible-web-mark:
Book forty-one in the World English Bible, Mark, announces good news immediately. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is its subject. Prophets foresaw a messenger preparing the way. A voice cries in the wilderness to make God's paths straight. John then appears, baptizing in that wilderness. He preaches repentance for forgiveness of sins.

Crowds from Judea and Jerusalem stream out to John. They confess sins and are baptized in the Jordan. John wears camel's hair and eats locusts and wild honey. He points to one mightier coming after him. Mark's pace stays breathless from this start. Readers get the shortest, sharpest telling of Jesus' ministry.
thomas-henry-huxley-a-sketch-of-his-life: P. Chalmers Mitchell wrote a sketch of Thomas Henry Huxley's life and work for the Leaders in Science series. G. P. Putnam's Sons published it in New York and London in 1900, printed by the Knickerbocker Press. A portrait illustration of Huxley opens the volume.
